At the beginning of 2025, it became clear that the style language has received many new features, which are already supported by modern browsers. In this article, we will review the most significant innovations that can simplify the work of developers and improve the user experience.\n\n## The balance value for the text-wrap property\n\nTypography has always been one of the most challenging tasks for web developers. One common problem is the uneven distribution of text in headers, especially on different devices. For example, when displaying long headers, it often happens that the last word stays on a separate line, negatively impacting the visual perception.\n\nTo solve this issue, the &#96;balance&#96; value is now available for the &#96;text-wrap&#96; property. It evenly distributes text across lines, minimizing the chance of lone words in a line. Example usage:\n\nh1 {\n  text-wrap: balance;\n}\n\nThis approach is especially useful for responsive design, where maintaining text readability on any screen size is important.\n\n**Example of property usage:** \n\n  \nTest code at separate page \n\n## Native CSS Nesting\n\nFor a long time, developers have used preprocessors like SASS or LESS for CSS rule nesting. However, in 2025, CSS introduced native support for nesting. Now, you can write code in this style:\n\n.awesome-block {\n  border: 2px solid lightblue;\n  padding: 1rem;\n   \n  \u0026:hover {\n    background-color: tomato;\n  }\n}\n\nThis syntax simplifies the structure of styles and makes the code more readable. However, it's important to be cautious when using the ampersand (&#96;\u0026&#96;) in class names, as it could cause errors.\n\n## The :user-valid and :user-invalid pseudo-classes\n\nWorking with forms has become even more convenient thanks to the new &#96;:user-valid&#96; and &#96;:user-invalid&#96; pseudo-classes. Unlike the traditional &#96;:valid&#96; and &#96;:invalid&#96;, which apply styles immediately after the page loads, the new pseudo-classes are triggered only after user interaction with the input field. This prevents unwanted visual effects during the page load phase.\n\n**Example of usage:** \n\ninput:user-invalid {\n  box-shadow: 0 0 10px red;\n}\n\ninput:user-valid {\n  box-shadow: 0 0 10px green;\n}\n\n**Example of usage:** \n\nTest code at separate page\n\n\u003e **Important!** The &#96;:user-valid&#96; and &#96;:user-invalid&#96; pseudo-classes are not yet supported by most browsers. As a result, styles may apply immediately upon page load (as with &#96;:valid&#96; and &#96;:invalid&#96;). To avoid this, you can use &#96;:focus&#96;, &#96;:focus-within&#96;, or add a handler using JavaScript.\n\n## The scrollbar-gutter property\n\nOne common issue when working with modal windows is the \"jumping\" of content caused by the appearance or disappearance of the scrollbar. The new &#96;scrollbar-gutter&#96; property allows you to reserve space for the scrollbar in advance, preventing content shifts.\n\n**Example:** \n\nhtml,\nbody {\n  scrollbar-gutter: stable;\n}\n\nThis solution is especially useful for improving the user experience when working with modal windows and other interface elements.\n\n## The round() mathematical function\n\nCSS now allows rounding values with the &#96;round()&#96; function. This is especially useful when working with non-integer values that may arise in layout. **Example:** \n\n.box {\n  margin: round(to-zero, 1.25rem, 1px);\n}\n\nThe &#96;round()&#96; function can be used in conjunction with &#96;calc()&#96;, making it a powerful tool for precise control over sizes and spacing.\n\n## The safe and unsafe keywords\n\nWhen using the &#96;align-items&#96; and &#96;justify-content&#96; properties, there can be cases where elements get cut off due to overflow in the container. The new &#96;safe&#96; and &#96;unsafe&#96; keywords allow you to control this behavior. For example:\n\n.parent {\n  align-items: safe center;\n}\n\nThe &#96;safe&#96; keyword ensures that elements will not be cut off at the start of the container, which is especially important for responsive interfaces.\n\n## The align-content property without the need for flexbox\n\nPreviously, in order to use the &#96;align-content&#96; property, you had to set the &#96;display&#96; property to &#96;flex&#96;, &#96;inline-flex&#96;, &#96;grid&#96;, or &#96;inline-grid&#96;. Now, &#96;align-content&#96; can function on its own, making it easier to center elements vertically. Example:\n\n.container {\n  height: 10rem;\n  background-color: lightblue;\n  align-content: center;\n}\n\n**The standard way of vertically aligning a block with &#96;display: flex&#96;:** \n\nTest code at separate page \n\n**And an example of how to vertically align a block using only &#96;align-content&#96;:** \n\nTest code at separate page \n\n\u003e **Important to note!** This property may not work in mobile browsers at the moment. You should use the method with the parameter &#96;display: flex&#96;.\n\nIt's important to note that blocks inside the container are not necessarily placed in a single line, but they will align vertically. To align &#96;items&#96; elements, simply apply &#96;float: left&#96;;.\n\n## Conclusion\n\nIn 2025, CSS continues to evolve, providing developers with new tools for creating more flexible and adaptive interfaces. Some of the most useful innovations include:\n\n* The &#96;balance&#96; value for the &#96;text-wrap&#96; property;\n* Native CSS nesting;\n* The &#96;:user-valid&#96; and &#96;:user-invalid&#96; pseudo-classes;\n* The &#96;scrollbar-gutter&#96; property;\n* The &#96;round()&#96; mathematical function.\n\nThese changes not only simplify the development process but also open new possibilities for creating higher-quality user interfaces. It's recommended to explore these features and begin using them in your projects.\n\nOther additional properties worth mentioning include:\n\n* The &#96;cap&#96; unit, based on the height of capital checkout previous years2023and2024where I shared snippets for those years.\n\nThis year, the snippets are bigger, more powerful, and leverage progressive enhancement a bit more; to help us step up to the **vast UI/UX requirements of 2025**.\n\n##  Springy easing with &#96;linear()&#96; # \n\nSprinkle life into animations with natural looking spring and bounce easings using &#96;linear()&#96;.\n\nUsing a series of linear lines to make \"curves\", you can create surprisingly realistic visual physics. **A small amount can go a long way** to addinginterest and intrigue to the user experience.\n\nIn the following video, the top animation uses &#96;ease-out&#96; and the bottom uses&#96;linear()&#96;, and I think the results are quite different, the bottom being more desirable.\n\nHere's some typical &#96;linear()&#96; easing CSS 😅:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.springy {\n  transition: transform 1s\n    linear(\n      0,\n      0.009,\n      0.035 2.1%,\n      0.141,\n      0.281 6.7%,\n      0.723 12.9%,\n      0.938 16.7%,\n      1.017,\n      1.077,\n      1.121,\n      1.149 24.3%,\n      1.159,\n      1.163,\n      1.161,\n      1.154 29.9%,\n      1.129 32.8%,\n      1.051 39.6%,\n      1.017 43.1%,\n      0.991,\n      0.977 51%,\n      0.974 53.8%,\n      0.975 57.1%,\n      0.997 69.8%,\n      1.003 76.9%,\n      1.004 83.8%,\n      1\n    );\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYes… that's what your formatter will do to it, as if it's helpful in some way lol.\n\nThe &#96;linear()&#96; code above is not very human readable, but the machines love it. No frets, there's a few generators out there:\n\n* \u003chttps://linear-easing-generator.netlify.app\u003e\n* \u003chttps://easingwizard.com\u003e\n\n**Tip!**  \nExpect longer durations when using &#96;linear()&#96;. When things run long, it can be nice to make them seamlessly interruptible, making &#96;linear()&#96; a great fit for transitions and potentially troublesome as keyframes.\n\nYou could alternatively use premade CSS variables from a library likeOpen Props:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@import \"https://unpkg.com/open-props/easings.min.css\";\n\n.springy {\n  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {\n    transition: transform 1s var(--ease-spring-3);\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEasy CSS to read, comes with 5 strengths for common effects:\n\nTry it\n\nTry the **Open Props Springs** notebook!\n\n###  Incrementally adopt# \n\nThis one is super easy to toss in today.\n\nEasiest way, use the cascade (if you're into that):\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {\n  /* just repeat the shorthand with adjusted easing */\n  .thingy {\n    transition: transform 0.3s ease;\n    transition: transform 0.3s linear(…);\n  }\n\n  /* or, target a specific property */\n  .thingy {\n    animation-timing-function: var(--ease-1);\n    animation-timing-function: var(--ease-spring-2);\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n**If it knows, it knows.**\n\nOr, test for it first and scalpel apply the upgrade:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.thingy {\n  transition: transform 0.3s ease;\n\n  @supports (transition-timing-function: linear(0, 0.1, 1)) {\n    transition-timing-function: var(--ease-spring-2);\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n##  Typed custom properties# \n\nSimilar to JS variables defined with &#96;var&#96;, CSS variables defined with &#96;--&#96; are global, loose, dynamic and flexible. This is great.\n\nBut… there are times, **like when building a system**, that you want to limit what goes into variables so a system can run with a reasonable amount of reliability.\n\nTry it\n\nIn the above video, a variable is set to an invalid color. At first, this breaks the system. But, @property is added, the system remained functioning with the latest known valid color value.\n\nCreate a typed &#96;\u003ccolor\u003e&#96; CSS variable like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: rebeccapurple;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn addition to type safety, &#96;@property&#96; defined variables can also be animated because the browser can infer the steps needed to interpolate the value change based on the assigned type.\n\nBefore &#96;@property&#96;, the browser couldn’t derive a type and discover interpolation steps, it was too complicated. Now, you give the browser a hint, and it's simple.\n\nIn 2025, y'all front-end devs should be getting familiar with defining variables with &#96;@property&#96; because it:\n\n1. Formalizes CSS system interfaces\n2. Protects CSS systems\n3. Enables new animation powers\n4. Can perform better when using&#96;inherits: false&#96;\nResources \n* \u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/vYPdBOO\u003e\n* \u003chttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSfSY3Ni3X0\u0026t=3409s\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/cant-break-this-design-system\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/type-guarded-css-systems-with-@property\u003e\n* \u003chttps://www.epicweb.dev/talks/lightning-in-a-bottle-with-css-custom-properties\u003e\n* \u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/MWZMxNN\u003e\n\n##  View transitions for page navigation# \n\nY'all should know how to crossfade pages when links are clicked with this tiny view transitions snippet:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@view-transition {\n  navigation: auto;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\n**This is the easiest snippet to add to your site, with no downsides.**\n\nIt signals your website would like to use page transitions when links are clicked, and the default transition is a crossfade.\n\nIf the browser doesn't support it, it continues as it always has; but if it does support it then you dab the page with some special sauce.\n\nThere's plenty more customization you can do, likefull page animations. But the gist of this section is just to share that easy snippet and the way the feature can be progressively enhanced.\n\n###  Incrementally adopt# \n\nThere's many more opportunities to add additional animations with the page transition.\n\nA great place to start enhancing this page transition experience is to identify elements commonly found across pages, and give them a &#96;name&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.nav {\n  view-transition-name: --nav;\n}\n\n.sidenav {\n  view-transition-name: --sidenav;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n**This includes elements in the page transition.**\n\nThey can even be different elements.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\na, h1 {\n  view-transition-name: --morphy;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nBy giving an &#96;\u003ca\u003e&#96; and an &#96;\u003ch1\u003e&#96; the sameview-transition-nameon two different pages, the browser will move and resize the page 1 element to the location and size of the page 2 element, making it look like a morph. You can of course morph between the same elements also.\n\nTry it\n\nThere is so much more. Continue giving elements names and studying therad examples by Bramus, and you can create experiences with motion like this:\n\nTry it\n\nI love theDevTools for Animations, scrubbing that full page view transition is very satisfying, and excellent for really inspecting and improving the little details.\n\nResources \n* Multi-page application View Transitions are here\n* Modern CSS for Sites Workshop\n* The CSS Podcast - #89 on View Transitions\n* Full page transitions starter\n* Bramus with a kit for IE Page-like Transitions\n\n##  Transition animation for &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; and &#96;[popover]&#96; # \n\nIn 2025, knowing your way around a\u003cdialog\u003eand a\\[popover\\]are table stakes. Otherwise, everyone else will be on top of you, and your wack&#96;z-index&#96; attempts will be defeated with a puny value of &#96;1&#96;.\n\nThese are common UI elements, with no JavaScript to download, and accessibility built in. **Use em** andknow the differences.\n\nThese two elements are projected into a layer above all the other UI called thetop layer. The browser projects the elements from anywhere in the document, to the top when shown.\n\n**To transition this**, there’s a few new CSS properties, for the full_interruptible_ CSS transition user experience —transition-behavior, the@starting-stylerule, and overlay.\n\nCombining these can feel like an incantation, but that makes it great copy and paste. So here! Use the following snippet to enable cross fade transitions for both &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; and &#96;popover&#96;:Try it\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n/* enable transitions, allow-discrete, define timing */\n[popover], dialog, ::backdrop {\n  transition: display 1s allow-discrete, overlay 1s allow-discrete, opacity 1s;\n  opacity: 0;\n}\n\n/* ON STAGE */\n:popover-open,\n:popover-open::backdrop,\n[open],\n[open]::backdrop {\n  opacity: 1;\n}\n\n/* OFF STAGE */\n/* starting-style for pre-positioning (enter stage from here) */\n@starting-style {\n  :popover-open,\n  :popover-open::backdrop,\n  [open],\n  [open]::backdrop {\n    opacity: 0;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhile this code is effective and terse, it's often not enough customization if you want to present and dismiss dialogs differently than you do popovers. Or make the entry animation different then the exit.\n\n###  Transition a dialog# \n\nHere's a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element with this barebones snippet applied. They look pretty terrible out of the box, but you cando amazing things with them.\n\nTry it\n\nTo get started, a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element needs to be in the HTML. A &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96;should be shown and hidden with buttons, one to show it can be in the page and one to close it should be inside the dialog.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cbutton onclick=\"demo.showModal()\"\u003e…\u003c/button\u003e\n\n\u003cdialog id=\"demo\"\u003e\n  \u003cheader\u003e\n    \u003cbutton title=\"Close\" onclick=\"demo.close()\"\u003eclose\u003c/button\u003e\n  \u003c/header\u003e\n\u003c/dialog\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can enable **light dismiss** on a dialog and skip the close button like&#96;\u003cdialog closedby=\"any\"\u003e&#96;\n\nTo animate the dialog transition:\n\n1. Two parts need animation: the &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; itself and its::backdrop.\n2. When a dialog is shown, &#96;display: none&#96; is changed to &#96;display: block&#96; andtransition-behaviorenables timing this change with our animation.\n3. When a dialog is shown, it is cloned into thetop layer, this also needs to be timed with our animation.\n4. The\\[open\\]attribute is used to know when the dialog is open or closed.@starting-styleis used during the first render as starting styles.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\ndialog {\n  /* Exit Stage To */\n  transform: translateY(-20px);\n\n  \u0026, \u0026::backdrop {\n    transition:\n      display 1s allow-discrete,\n      overlay 1s allow-discrete,\n      opacity 1s ease,\n      transform 1s ease;\n\n    /* Exit Stage To */\n    opacity: 0;\n  }\n\n  /* On Stage */\n  \u0026[open] {\n    opacity: 1;\n    transform: translateY(0px);\n\n    \u0026::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0.8;\n    }\n  }\n\n  /* Enter Stage From */\n  @starting-style {\n    \u0026[open],\n    \u0026[open]::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0;\n    }\n\n    \u0026[open] {\n      transform: translateY(20px);\n    }\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\nWith this snippet as a starting point, you can find three popular dialog experiences for you to take code or inspiration from/have-a-dialog.\n\nThe following video shows the excellent keyboard experience. It also demonstrates the interruptible nature of a CSS transition, so a user can close it anytime they want and always see a smooth interface.\n\nnerdy.dev/have-a-dialog\n\nResources \n* \u003chttps://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLDialogElement\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/notebook/dialog-starter.html\u003e\n* \u003chttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yORy1IEHDKk\u003e\n* \u003chttps://web.dev/blog/baseline-entry-animations\u003e\n* Pop n' Lock Dialog Mini Web Machine\n\n###  Transition a popover# \n\nLike a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element, a popover appears over everything else in the top layer. Light dismiss is the default, and keyboard / focus management is all done for you.\n\n\u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/mdZXzxW\u003e\n\n**Let's bulid it.**\n\nThere's an HTML aspect to implementing the UX:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cbutton popovertarget=\"pop\"\u003e?\u003c/button\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"pop\" popover\u003eAn overlay with additional information.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nAlso, like a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element, to animate the transition of a popover's display property and insertion into the top layer, you need to combine&#96;transition-behavior&#96; and &#96;@starting-style&#96;.\n\nNotice with a popover, the open state isn't an attribute, it's a css pseudo-class &#96;:popover-open&#96;.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n[popover] {\n  \u0026, \u0026::backdrop {\n    transition:\n      display 0.5s allow-discrete,\n      overlay 0.5s allow-discrete,\n      opacity 0.5s,\n      transform 0.5s;\n\n    /* Exit Stage To */\n    opacity: 0;\n  }\n\n  /* On Stage */\n  \u0026:popover-open {\n    opacity: 1;\n\n    \u0026::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0.5;\n    }\n  }\n\n  /* Enter Stage From */\n  @starting-style {\n    \u0026:popover-open,\n    \u0026:popover-open::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0;\n    }\n\n    \u0026:popover-open {\n      transform: translateY(10px);\n    }\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\nResources \n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/steal-this-popover-starter-kit\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/notebook/dialog-starter.html\u003e\n* \u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/entry-exit-animations\u003e\n* \u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/css-ui-ecommerce-popover\u003e\n* Over-Easy Anchor + Popover Mini Web Machine\n\n##  Transition animation for &#96;\u003cdetails\u003e&#96; # \n\nFound on the CSS Wrapped 2024 website in the desktop layout.\n\nThe disclosure element (&#96;\u003cdetails\u003e&#96;) has been waiting for CSS primitives to unlock its animation potential for many years.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cdetails\u003e\n  \u003csummary\u003eShow disclosed content\u003c/summary\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/details\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe details element needs to transition to &#96;height: auto&#96; from &#96;height: 0px&#96; and a way to target the slotted content it internally uses for the disclosure. The newinterpolate-sizefeature can be used for the height animation and::details-content for the selector.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\ndetails {\n  inline-size: 50ch;\n\n  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {\n    interpolate-size: allow-keywords;\n  }\n\n  \u0026::details-content {\n    opacity: 0;\n    block-size: 0;\n    overflow-y: clip;\n    transition: content-visibility 1s allow-discrete, opacity 1s, block-size 1s;\n  }\n\n  \u0026[open]::details-content {\n    opacity: 1;\n    block-size: auto;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\nResources \n* \u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/styling-details\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/open-and-close-transitions-for-the-details-element\u003e\n* \u003chttps://css-tricks.com/almanac/pseudo-selectors/d/details-content/\u003e\n\n###  Bonus attribute# \n\nIf you want to connect two or more details elements and have them close each other respectively, you can accomplish this with a sharednameattribute on each detail element you want to be connected. Very much like aradio group.\n\n\u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/styling-details\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cdetails name=\"linked-disclosure\"\u003e\n  \u003csummary\u003eShow disclosed content\u003c/summary\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/details\u003e\n\n\u003c!-- name=\"linked-disclosure\" connects these together --\u003e\n\n\u003cdetails name=\"linked-disclosure\u003e\n  \u003csummary\u003eShow disclosed content\u003c/summary\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/details\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n##  Animated adaptive gradient text# \n\nA bold headline in a design is often complimented with a gradient, helping draw the eye with intrigue and vividness.\n\nSince 2015 the web has been able to create gradient text effects, and in the past 10 years, there have been some updates and enhancements: animation, user preferences and interpolation.\n\n1. Adapting the gradient text effect to **light and dark themes** is easy with the &#96;prefers-color-scheme&#96; query\n2. New animation updates enable gradient effects to **go beyond spinning or moving gradient images around**, but to change colors over time\n3. New interpolation updates allow those **mixes to be more vivid, rich, and interesting**\n\n\u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/vEBmZNw\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@property --color-2 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@keyframes color-change {\n  to {\n    --color-1: var(--_color-1-to);\n    --color-2: var(--_color-2-to);\n  }\n}\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_space: ;\n\n  /* light mode */\n  --_color-1-from: yellow;\n  --_color-1-to: orange;\n  --_color-2-from: purple;\n  --_color-2-to: hotpink;\n\n  /* dark mode */\n  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {\n    --_color-1-from: lime;\n    --_color-1-to: cyan;\n    --_color-2-from: cyan;\n    --_color-2-to: deeppink;\n  }\n\n  --color-1: var(--_color-1-from);\n  --color-2: var(--_color-2-from);\n\n  animation: color-change 2s linear infinite alternate;\n\n  background: linear-gradient(\n    to right var(--_space),\n    var(--color-1),\n    var(--color-2)\n  );\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n\n  @supports (background: linear-gradient(in oklch, #fff, #fff)) {\n    --_space: in oklch;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThat's quite a snippet 😅 How did it get to that?\n\nMost developers making a gradient text effect are starting here:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  background: linear-gradient(to right, hotpink, cyan);\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  remove the prefixes# \n\nThe first update or enhancement is to remove the prefixes. Although, so older browsers continue to support the effect, add the unprefixed values after:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  background: linear-gradient(to right, hotpink, cyan);\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  Use updated gradient interpolation spaces# \n\nNext, improve the quality of the gradient by progressively enhancing the &#96;in&#96; interpolation syntaxwith CSS variables and &#96;@supports&#96;.\n\nYou could alternatively repeat the gradient definition and include &#96;in oklch&#96; in it, which would also work great and support older browsers.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_space: ;\n\n  background: linear-gradient(to right var(--_space), hotpink, cyan);\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n\n  @supports (background: linear-gradient(in oklch, #fff, #fff)) {\n    --_space: in oklch;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  Create typed &#96;\u003ccolor\u003e&#96; properties# \n\nFor the gradient color animation use &#96;@property&#96;, like described in snippet #4\\. The typed color values can be animated inside of a gradient, like a gradient used with text.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@property --color-2 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNow &#96;--color-1&#96; can be animated like &#96;transition: –color-1 .3s ease&#96; or used in keyframes. These values that can animate, can be used anywhere color is allowed, like in a gradient text effect.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@keyframes color-change {\n  to {\n    --color-1: lime --color-2: orange;\n  }\n}\n\n.gradient-text {\n  animation: color-change 2s linear infinite alternate;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  Make a few props, Swap em' in a dark MQ# \n\nTo keep things declarative, I've also defined color variables to hold the colors for animation.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_color-1-from: yellow;\n  --_color-1-to: orange;\n  --_color-2-from: purple;\n  --_color-2-to: hotpink;\n\n  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {\n    --_color-1-from: lime;\n    --_color-1-to: cyan;\n    --_color-2-from: cyan;\n    --_color-2-to: deeppink;\n  }\n\n  /* set our typed variables to the \"from\" values */\n  --color-1: var(--_color-1-from);\n  --color-2: var(--_color-2-from);\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nPut all those moments and reasons together, and we have arrived at the final snippet:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@property --color-2 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@keyframes color-change {\n  to {\n    --color-1: var(--_color-1-to);\n    --color-2: var(--_color-2-to);\n  }\n}\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_space: ;\n\n  /* light mode */\n  --_color-1-from: yellow;\n  --_color-1-to: orange;\n  --_color-2-from: purple;\n  --_color-2-to: hotpink;\n\n  /* dark mode */\n  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {\n    --_color-1-from: lime;\n    --_color-1-to: cyan;\n    --_color-2-from: cyan;\n    --_color-2-to: deeppink;\n  }\n\n  --color-1: var(--_color-1-from);\n  --color-2: var(--_color-2-from);\n\n  animation: color-change 2s linear infinite alternate;\n\n  background: linear-gradient(\n    to right var(--_space),\n    var(--color-1),\n    var(--color-2)\n  );\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n\n  @supports (background: linear-gradient(in oklch, #fff, #fff)) {\n    --_space: in oklch;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n🤓 \n\nSome years these snippets are short and sweet, but not this year.       "chunk": "ARTLUNG. photo of Joe at the beach, plus inset picture of Woody Guthrie's hands on his guitar with a signing reading THIS MACHINE KILLS FASCISTS. Plus watercolor flags of Ukraine and Palestine.\n\n* ArtLung\n* blog\n* 2025\n* 06\n* 02\n* Here\n\n# “📣 YouTube removed your content” (A Google Mystery) \n\nA few weeks ago, on Wednesday, May 21, 8:56 AM I got this email:\n\n\u003e YouTube\n\u003e \n\u003e Hi Joe Crawford,\n\u003e \n\u003e It looks like an external link you included in **CSSBattle for DECEMBER 5 (2024) Logo-i-zer \u0026 ArtLung Lab** didn’t follow Community Guidelines. To help keep our community safe, we removed your content from YouTube.\n\u003e \n\u003e **External link:** https://apps.artlung.com/logo-i-zer/create.php\n\u003e \n\u003e REVIEW AND TAKE ACTION\n\u003e \n\u003e Warning\n\u003e \n\u003e **What we found**\n\u003e \n\u003e We think your content didn’t follow our harmful and dangerous policy.\n\u003e \n\u003e External links that go to sites that contain spam, scams, or other deceptive practices aren’t allowed on YouTube. Read policy\n\u003e \n\u003e **How this impacts you**\n\u003e \n\u003e This is just a warning. Because this is your first time, you can still upload, post, and live stream. However, we removed your content from YouTube.\n\u003e \n\u003e **What to do next**\n\u003e \n\u003e Review your content and the policy. After your review, you can appeal if you think we got it wrong, and you can take an optional training to remove the warning. Learn about your resolution options.\n\u003e \n\u003e **How we find violations**\n\u003e \n\u003e We use a combination of automated systems and human reviews to detect violations of our Community Guidelines.\n\u003e \n\u003e Thanks,  \n\u003e The YouTube Team\n\nIt had the subject **“📣 YouTube removed your content”**\n\nI was quite surprised by this email. This was indeed for my video entitled CSSBattle for DECEMBER 5 (2024) Logo-i-zer \u0026 ArtLung Lab. This video:\n\n---\n\nI also had another email in my inbox. This one had the title **“Social engineering content detected on https://artlung\\[.\\]com/”** with a timestamp of May 21, 2025, 10:34 AM.\n\n\u003e **Social engineering content detected on https://artlung.com/**\n\u003e \n\u003e Google’s Safe Browsing systems have detected that some pages on your site might be hacked or might include third party resources such as ads that are designed to trick users into installing malicious software or giving up sensitive information. To protect your site’s visitors, affected pages have been demoted in Google’s search results, and browsers such as Google Chrome now display a warning when users visit your site. You can see which pages might be affected in the Security Issues report.\n\u003e \n\u003e Act now to fix this problem and remove the warning:\n\u003e \n\u003e 1. **Identify compromised pages**  \n\u003e Check the example URLs in the “Security Issues” page in Search Console. Note that this page displays a list of samples and not an exhaustive list of problematic URLs.  \n\u003e View examples\n\u003e 2. **Remove the deceptive content**  \n\u003e If you’re having trouble identifying and removing all the problematic content on your site, consider restoring an older version of your site. If you have ads on your site, ensure that they are not designed to trick or deceive visitors.\n\u003e 3. **Secure your site from any future attacks**  \n\u003e Identify and fix any vulnerabilities that caused your site to be compromised. Change passwords for administrative accounts. Consider contacting your hosting service to assist with the issue.\n\u003e 4. **Request a security review**  \n\u003e Only do this once you’re sure your site is free of problematic content. Include any details or documentation that can help understand the changes made to your site.Request a review\n\u003e 5. Here is a sample of URLs from your site where we detected social engineering content:&#96;http://apps.artlung[.]com/&#96;  \n\u003e &#96;http://artlung[.]com/logo-i-zer/&#96;\n\u003e \n\u003e **Need more help?**\n\u003e \n\u003e * Learn more about Phishing and Social Engineering.\n\u003e * Read our help guide for hacked sites.\n\u003e * Learn how to request a review in our help center.\n\u003e * Ask questions in our forum for more help – mention message type \\[WNC-806900\\].\n\nThis alarmed me MUCH MORE. One video taken down is bad. But a whole domain of mine – not my main domain, but my “apps” subdomain marked as dangerous was troubling.\n\nGoogle has detected harmful content on some of your site’s pages. We recommend that you remove it as soon as possible. Until then, browsers such as Google Chrome will display a warning when users visit or download certain files from your site. These pages attempt to trick users into doing something dangerous, such as installing unwanted software or revealing personal information.\n\nFirefox and Chrome and Safari all had flagged that domain with that BIG RED BLOCKING PAGE blocking entry unless you are really really sure.\n\nMy friend gRegor shared that he saw this in Chrome blog tools:\n\n\u003e Chrome is blocking ads on this site because this site tends to show ads that interrupt, distract, mislead, or prevent user control. You should fix the issues as soon as possible and submit your site for another review. Learn more at \u003chttps://www.chromestatus.com/feature/5738264052891648\u003e\n\n---\n\n## What on earth is going on?\n\nI had no idea what was going. I thought it was possible that my site had been infected with malware. Or maybe some other chunk of content on my site had been altered by a malicious actor.\n\nI downloaded a fresh copy of all the files for whole domain &#96;apps.artlung.com&#96;. I inspected it all locally.\n\nI keep a copy of everything there in a source code repository (git) and there were a few changes. Some temp files I had shared with friends. Minor updates. But nothing malicious. Nothing suspicious.\n\nI reran the &#96;rsync&#96; to doublecheck I hadn’t missed anything that might be _hiding_ and again came up empty.\n\nI mentioned this in the IndieWeb Homebrew Website Club meeting that day. Mark recommended a PHP malware scanner. I used that to do some scans, locally. Nothing bad. And on the hosting server, nothing I could find.\n\nI re-read the emails from Google and YouTube. I looked inside Google Search Console.\n\nI originally authenticated with Google Search Console tool using a DNS record a few years ago. It covers everything on the artlung.com domain. If you’ve been making web pages you might remember adding a file like google123123123.html to your site to verify it. It’s like that. In theory it lets you see what the search engine sees about a website.\n\nAnd I looked again at the page in question and looked at the source code.\n\nThe code solicits user input. The code also stores user choices: two colors.\n\nThat’s it. And it makes a logo (my logo) from the colors.\n\nBut it does invite users to do something.\n\n## I develop a theory and a possible solution\n\nHaving a website marked as dangerous by a Google means that the whole domain might get big warning block screens added. Users can go by it? But they ought not to. It was in my interest to fix it.\n\nI read closer what the problems were. I decided that I needed to add a few things:\n\n* a description of precisely what the page is\n* links to all related pages for the site\n* a privacy policy (an assurance I am not gathering information)\n* a terms of service (what guarantees I have to make about the site)\n\n## Implementing solutions\n\nAnd in an hour or so I’d done that. It looked roughly like it does now:\n\nscreenshot of https://apps.artlung.com/logo-i-zer/create.php\n\nThis included a **Privacy Policy**:\n\n\u003e LOGO-I-ZER does not collect any personal information of any kind and does not retain any information about your use of the tool. The only items retained are the images created based on the two image colors. The resulting image sets the “ARTLUNG” logo with the foreground and background colors selected.\n\u003e \n\u003e No cookies or sessionStorage are used. localStorage is used to retain the last 2 colors you chose on the Create page.\n\nAnd a very basic **Terms of Service** page:\n\n\u003e Service is provided “as is” without warranty of any kind. Use at your own risk.\n\n## Asking for a review of my changes in Google\n\nInside Google Search Console I submitted a request to re-review the site. My supporting text was this:\n\n\u003e I believe the issue may have been that my page was not clear about what it is and does. The page allows users to choose two colors to set my logo in, and uses localStorage to retain those choices for the user. I have added a privacy policy communicating that fact, and a terms of service page.\n\n## Asking for a review of my changes in YouTube\n\nI did the same thing inside YouTube, to address the fact that in the console for my videos that video was marked as disabled.\n\nI also was given the chance to take a short training course for how to behave properly inside YouTube. When creators you watch on YouTube mention demonetization, or takedowns, this all seems related. It asked me questions about how to represent the truth, not advocate for bad behavior, and a few other topics. It was very much like the kind of Human Resources most folks who have worked a job have had to do.\n\nThe training took me half an hour, and I passed.\n\nPolicy training Nice work! You've completed the training We appreciate you taking the time to help us keep YouTube safe. Check out our Community Guldellnes any time you re unsure about posting content What's next? • Your warning will expire on Aug 19, 2025 • If you violate the Harmful or Dangerous policy again before this warning expires, you'll get a strike • If you violate a different policy, you'll get another warning with the opportunity to take another training.\n\n---\n\n## Ban Removed, Video Restored\n\nThe next day, actually in the early morning of May 22nd, maybe 8 hours later, I got this email:\n\n\u003e **Review successful for https://artlung.com/**\n\u003e \n\u003e To: Owner of https://artlung.com/,\n\u003e \n\u003e Google has received and processed your security review request. Google systems indicate that https://artlung.com/ no longer contains links to harmful sites or downloads. The warnings visible to users are being removed from your site. This may take a few hours to happen.\n\u003e \n\u003e **Here are ways to keep your site safe in the future:**\n\u003e \n\u003e 1. **Secure your site from any future attacks**  \n\u003e Identify and fix vulnerabilities that caused your site to be compromised. Change passwords for administrative accounts. Consider contacting your hosting service for assistance.\n\u003e 2. **Always follow the Unwanted Software Policy**  \n\u003e Make sure all downloadable files from your site comply with the criteria listed in the policy. Files that violate these criteria will be identified as unwanted software.  \n\u003e Read policy\n\u003e \n\u003e ---\n\u003e \n\u003e **Resources**\n\u003e \n\u003e Learn about preventing malware infection in our help center.  \n\u003e Ask questions in our forum (Mention message type \\[WNC-608000\\]).\n\nAnd James pointed out in the IndieWeb chat that:\n\n\u003e Your apps. subdomain is no longer being flagged by Google: \u003chttps://transparencyreport.google.com/safe-browsing/search?url=https:%2F%2Fapps.artlung.com\u0026hl=en%5FGB\u003e\n\n---\n\n## Takeaways\n\nThese were all automated messages. None of them seemed to _directly_ engage and point at a single “problem” with my sites that was triggering the flagging. But I’ll take a shot at some possible descriptive theories about how Google and YouTube work here in 2025:\n\n* Any link added to the description in a YouTube video probably gets additional scrutiny. I say that because to even add a single https link to my videos I had to do some identify verification with YouTube. HTTP links have power.\n* Any web page that has form inputs and is asking a user to do something and also saves data to localStorage probably ought to explain itself in plain language\n* Including a privacy policy is probably table stakes for any site that takes user input, no matter how trivial\n* Including a terms of service is not a bad idea\n* Google has a ton of power: once my site was flagged, Firefox, Chrome, and Safari all had BIG RED BLOCKING SCREENS in place for any usage of my subdomain with big nasty ARE YOU SURE warnings for anyone wanting to click through.\n* My case was specific, and none of the form emails I got seemed to really describe what was happening on the site. There’s such a panoply of ways a web page can be bad there’s no way to automate describing what’s suspicious about a website\n* Google followed up quickly to my request for review. And as soon as I got the email back from Google, my YouTube video was restored.\n* It’s helpful to have community to bounce ideas off. Huzzah my friends in the IndieWeb.\n* I keep learning new stuff from vlogging CSS Battles. Here were the lessons when I was at 110 Hours. (I’m at 116 hours now).\n\nTo quote Courtney Barnett:\n\n\u003e It’s a Monday / It’s so mundane / What exciting things’ll happen today?\n\nThanks for reading. I hope this will be helpful to someone in this scenario.\n\nJune 2 2025 google google search console programming webdev webmaster The Date  4 comments \n\nartlung Joe Crawford \n\nA few weeks ago, on Wednesday, May 21, 8:56 AM I got this email: Hi Joe Crawford, It looks like an external link you included in CSSBattle for DECEMBER 5 (2024) Logo-i-zer \u0026 ArtLung Lab didn’t follow Community Guidelines. + import * as React from "react";
+ import { cn } from "@/utils";
+ import { ClassificationLevel } from "./types";
+ 
+ interface VintageDocumentCardProps {
+   className?: string;
+   children: React.ReactNode;
+   classification: ClassificationLevel;
+   title: string;
+   date: string;
+   location?: string;
+ }
+ 
+ const ClassificationBadge = ({ level }: { level: ClassificationLevel }) =&gt; {
+   const getClassificationStyles = (classification: ClassificationLevel) =&gt; {
+     const baseStyles = "inline-block px-3 py-1 text-sm font-bold tracking-wider transform -rotate-3 border-2";
+     
+     switch (classification) {
+       case "top-secret":
+         return &#96;${baseStyles} bg-red-600 text-white border-red-800 shadow-red-900/30&#96;;
+       case "secret":
+         return &#96;${baseStyles} bg-orange-500 text-white border-orange-700 shadow-orange-800/30&#96;;
+       case "confidential":
+         return &#96;${baseStyles} bg-yellow-500 text-black border-yellow-700 shadow-yellow-800/30&#96;;
+       case "unclassified":
+         return &#96;${baseStyles} bg-green-600 text-white border-green-800 shadow-green-900/30&#96;;
+       default:
+         return &#96;${baseStyles} bg-gray-500 text-white border-gray-700 shadow-gray-800/30&#96;;
+     }
+   };
+ 
+   return (
+     &lt;div className="absolute top-4 right-4 z-10"&gt;
+       &lt;span className={cn(getClassificationStyles(level), "shadow-lg")}&gt;
+         {level.toUpperCase().replace("-", " ")}
+       &lt;/span&gt;
+     &lt;/div&gt;
+   );
+ };
+ 
+ const VintageDocumentCard = React.forwardRef&lt;HTMLDivElement, VintageDocumentCardProps&gt;(
+   ({ className, children, classification, title, date, location, ...props }, ref) =&gt; {
+     return (
+       &lt;div
+         ref={ref}
+         className={cn(
+           // Base vintage paper styling
+           "relative bg-amber-50 dark:bg-amber-100",
+           "border-2 border-amber-200 dark:border-amber-300",
+           "shadow-2xl",
+           // Aged paper effect
+           "before:absolute before:inset-0 before:bg-gradient-to-br before:from-transparent before:via-amber-100/20 before:to-amber-200/40",
+           "before:pointer-events-none before:rounded-lg",
+           // Slight paper curl effect
+           "after:absolute after:top-0 after:right-0 after:w-6 after:h-6",
+           "after:bg-gradient-to-br after:from-amber-200 after:to-amber-300",
+           "after:transform after:rotate-45 after:-translate-y-1 after:translate-x-1",
+           "after:shadow-md after:rounded-sm after:opacity-60",
+           // Paper texture simulation
+           "bg-[radial-gradient(circle_at_20%_20%,rgba(139,69,19,0.05)_0%,transparent_50%),radial-gradient(circle_at_80%_80%,rgba(139,69,19,0.05)_0%,transparent_50%)]",
+           // Overall card styling
+           "rounded-lg p-6 max-w-2xl mx-auto",
+           // Subtle aged spots
+           "shadow-[inset_0_0_20px_rgba(139,69,19,0.1)]",
+           className
+         )}
+         {...props}
+       &gt;
+         {/* Classification Badge */}
+         &lt;ClassificationBadge level={classification} /&gt;
+

        "contents": ".data-card {\n  flex: 1;\n  max-width: 430px;\n  min-width: 380px;\n  display: grid;\n  grid-template-columns: 1.2fr 1fr min-content;\n  grid-auto-rows: min-content;\n  background: #fdfdfd;\n  margin: 2rem;\n  line-height: 1.5;\n  position: relative;\n  box-shadow:\n    0 4px 0 -2px #ddd,\n    1px 1px 0 0 #f7f7f7;\n}\n\n.data-card:before,\n.data-card:after {\n  z-index: -1;\n  position: absolute;\n  content: '';\n  bottom: 35px;\n  left: 10px;\n  width: 50%;\n  top: 80%;\n  max-width: 300px;\n  background: #777;\n  box-shadow: 0 35px 20px #777;\n  transform: rotate(-4deg);\n}\n\n.data-card::after {\n  transform: rotate(4deg);\n  right: 10px;\n  left: auto;\n}\n\n.data-card\u003e* {\n  padding: 0.6rem 1.2rem;\n}\n\n.data-card h1 {\n  font-size: clamp(2.2rem, 4.2vw, 3rem);\n  line-height: 1;\n  font-weight: 500;\n}\n\n.data-card .name {\n  grid-column: 1/-1;\n  grid-row: 2;\n  padding-bottom: 1.2rem;\n}\n\n.data-card .info,\n.data-card .location,\n.data-card .type,\n.data-card .pattern {\n  grid-column: 1 / span 2;\n}\n\n.data-card .date,\n.data-card .weight {\n  transform: rotate(180deg);\n  writing-mode: vertical-lr;\n  padding: 1.2rem 0;\n}\n\n.data-card .date,\n.data-card .weight,\n.data-card .footnote,\n.data-card .site {\n  font-size: 85%;\n}\n\n.data-card .date {\n  grid-row: 3 / span 4;\n  grid-column: 3/4;\n}\n\n.data-card .footnote {\n  grid-column: 1/2;\n}\n\n.data-card .weight {\n  grid-row: 7 / span 1;\n  grid-column: 3/4;\n  min-height: 10rem;\n}\n\n.data-card .pattern {\n  grid-row: 6 / span 2;\n  min-height: 16.5rem;\n  background-repeat: repeat;\n}\n\n.side-title {\n  display: inline-block;\n  margin-bottom: 0.75rem;\n  border-bottom: 0.5px dashed;\n  padding: 0 0.8rem 0.75rem;\n}\n\n.data-card .name,\n.data-card .info,\n.data-card .location,\n.data-card .weight {\n  border-bottom: 0.5px dashed;\n}\n\n.data-card .info,\n.data-card .location,\n.data-card .type,\n.data-card .footnote {\n  border-right: 0.5px dashed;\n}\n\n.checkbox {\n  display: inline-block;\n  pointer-events: none;\n}\n\n.checkbox:nth-child(1) {\n  margin-right: 30px;\n}\n\n",

      "chunk": "May 28, 2025 by Sahil Lavingia\n\n# DOGE Days\n\nIn August 2014, President Obama and Congress created the United States Digital Service (USDS).\n\nIn January 2025, President Trump signed an executive order to rename and reorganize it as the United States DOGE Service.\n\n\u003e In consultation with USDS, each Agency Head shall establish within their respective Agencies a DOGE Team of at least four employees, which may include Special Government Employees, hired or assigned within thirty days of the date of this Order. Agency Heads shall select the DOGE Team members in consultation with the USDS Administrator. Each DOGE Team will typically include one DOGE Team Lead, one engineer, one human resources specialist, and one attorney. Agency Heads shall ensure that DOGE Team Leads coordinate their work with USDS and advise their respective Agency Heads on implementing the President's DOGE Agenda.\n\n— Executive Order 14123: Establishing and Implementing the President's Department of Government Efficiency (Federal Register)\n\nOn March 17 2025, I joined DOGE as a software engineer working for the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).\n\n## Day 0\n\nThe Friday before starting, I went to the VA Medical Center in Manhattan to get fingerprinted. While filling out forms, I left the \"employee/contractor/volunteer\" field blank because I didn't know the answer.\n\nI just knew I wanted to write code for the federal government. VA's impact is around $350 billion a year, with 473,000 employees.\n\nIn 2016, I canvassed for Bernie Sanders. I spent my first day in Nevada walking door-to-door in the desert heat with a dying phone battery and a stack of printed papers delineating potential voters, thinking \"there really should be an app for this.\" There, I ended up writing some Google Apps code for caucus result reporting.\n\nThis was a chance to do something bigger.\n\n## Day 1: March 17, 2025\n\nI arrived early at the VA Central Office in DC, got sworn in, received my government ID, and attended onboarding orientation. There, I learned my title, Senior Advisor to the Chief of Staff Christopher Syrek, and my salary, $0.\n\nMy first task involved reviewing contracts.\n\n\u003e Each Agency Head, in consultation with the agency's DOGE Team Lead, shall review all existing covered contracts and grants and, where appropriate and consistent with applicable law, terminate or modify (including through renegotiation) such covered contracts and grants to reduce overall Federal spending or reallocate spending to promote efficiency and advance the policies of my Administration.\n\n— Executive Order 14124: Implementing the President's Department of Government Efficiency Cost Efficiency Initiative (Federal Register)\n\nThe existing method was manual and tedious: finding PDFs, contacting responsible individuals, and determining necessity. VA had over 90,000 active contracts ranging from IT support to landscaping.\n\nTo streamline this, I proposed a simple script:\n\n* Iterate through contract PDFs\n* Extract the text\n* Utilize an LLM to flag for potential cancellation\n* Compile flagged contracts into a CSV for easy review\n\nI also suggested a dashboard where VA contracting officers could easily view flagged contracts.\n\n## Day 2\n\nWorking within the executive branch felt like working at a large tech company, except where business strategy was outsourced to Congress, and software engineering was outsourced to contractors like IBM, Accenture, Deloitte, and Booz Allen Hamilton.\n\nI was excited to help in-source VA's software, but I was also realizing why so much of it was outsourced. For example, I was constantly constrained by my restricted government laptop, which made it difficult to write and run code. I couldn't install Git, Python, or use tools like Cursor, due to government security policies.\n\nFixing the root of the problem–making it easier for employees to execute–would require congressional intervention, and it was more practical to continue spending lots of money outsourcing the software development to contractors.\n\n## Day 3\n\nMost of the day involved meetings about the upcoming Reduction in Force (RIF) with VA leadership, including Secretary Doug Collins and Chief of Staff Mark Engelbaum, to discuss plans for an organizational reorganization.\n\n\u003e Agency heads should collaborate with their Department of Government Efficiency (\"DOGE\") team leads within the agency in developing competitive areas for ARRPs.\n\n— Executive Order 14159: Implementing the President's Department of Government Efficiency Workforce Optimization Initiative (Federal Register)\n\nInitially, I expected multiple fragmented HR systems, but learned VA had already consolidated HR data within IBM's HR Smart. By late afternoon, I successfully extracted the necessary data and constructed an MVP org chart visualizer, representing the nearly half-million VA employees.\n\nThen came a reality check about RIF rules, which turned out to be brutally deterministic:\n\n* Tenure matters most—new hires were cut first\n* Veterans' preference comes next; vets are protected over non-vets\n* Length of service trumps performance—seniority beats skill\n* Performance ratings break any remaining ties\n\nThese reduction-in-force rules–which stem from the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944–surprised me and many others. Unlike private industry layoffs that target middle management bloat and low performers, the government cuts its newest people first, regardless of performance. Anyone promoted within the last two years was also considered probationary—first in line to go.\n\n## Day 5\n\nIn meetings with the Office of the CTO, I discovered ambitious ongoing software projects like reducing veterans' benefits claims processing from 133 days to under a week. I also learned that several of VA's code repos were already open-source, and the world's first electronic health record system, VistA, was built by VA employees over 40 years ago.\n\nMaybe the government _could_ in-source and open-source its software stack after all.\n\nI also learned that my frustrations with the government laptop_were_ solvable; Charles Worthington, VA's CTO, recommended getting a software engineering-grade MacBook.\n\nI wondered why there wasn't a centralized DOGE software engineering playbook with all of our learnings; overall, I was surprised by the lack of knowledge-sharing within DOGE. It seemed like every engineer started from scratch.\n\n## Day 8\n\nThe reality was setting in: DOGE was more like having McKinsey volunteers embedded in agencies rather than the revolutionary force I'd imagined. It was Elon (in the White House), Steven Davis (coordinating), and everyone else scattered across agencies.\n\nMeanwhile, the public was seeing news reports of mass firings that seemed cruel and heartless, many assuming DOGE was directly responsible.\n\nIn reality, DOGE had no direct authority. The real decisions came from the agency heads appointed by President Trump, who were wise to let DOGE act as the 'fall guy' for unpopular decisions.\n\n## Day 13\n\nI attended my first and last DOGE all-hands. It felt like a candid Q\u0026A with Elon rather than a structured meeting. When he asked the room about improving DOGE's public perception, I asked if I could open-source the code I'd been writing. He said yes–it aligned with DOGE's goal of maximum transparency.\n\nThe code is on GitHub here.\n\n## Day 21: April 1, 2025\n\nI returned home to New York to work remotely out of the basement of the Manhattan VA Medical Center.\n\nAlthough DOGE hadn't met my expectations of a cohesive team culture, I felt optimistic about my individual impact at VA. I had many ideas on how to improve veterans' care while saving money with software, and the assigned work of cutting contracts, helping RIF, and providing technical advice didn't take up much of my time.\n\nI started to work on two VA-specific projects:\n\n* Modernizing our internal version of ChatGPT (called VAGPT)\n* An AI chatbot that could help veterans get help when visiting VA.gov\n\n## Day 34\n\nI completed the migration of VAGPT to a more modern front-end consisting of NextJS, Tailwind, ShadCN. Most importantly, I made it mobile responsive.\n\nLoading...\n\nI also got buy-in from VA on open-sourcing the VAGPT repo, so that other federal agencies can benefit from the same code for free. It also meant non-government employees–like me, eventually–could chip in.\n\nLastly, we planned a hackathon for the new AI chatbot to start on May 19, 2025.\n\n## Day 55: May 9, 2025\n\nI got the boot from DOGE.\n\nI reached out to someone who wrote about Gumroad's recent transition to open source. During the interview, which was then published in Fast Company, I was asked about my experience working at DOGE, which had been revealed publicly as part of a WIRED article.\n\nSoon after publication, my access was revoked without warning.\n\nMy DOGE days were over.\n\n## What did I get done?\n\n* Wrote a contract analysis script using LLMs to flag wasteful spending\n* Deployed a productized version of the contract analysis tool within the VA cloud\n* Built org chart tools: Interactive visualizations to aid RIF execution for 473,000 employees\n* Modernized our internal ChatGPT, VAGPT\n* Shipped a VA Chatbot demo for VA.gov, for helping veterans navigate services\n* Sped up AI adoption: According to a VA engineer, accelerated adoption by \"12 months\"\n\nIn the end, I learned a lot, and got to write some code for the federal government. For that, I'm grateful.\n\nBut I'm also disappointed. I didn't make any progress on improving the UX of veterans' filing disability claims or automating/speeding up claims processing, like I had hoped to when I started. I built several prototypes, but was never able to get approval to ship anything to production that would actually improve American lives–while also saving money for the American taxpayer.\n\nMaybe next time.\n\nDepartment of Government Efficiency\n\nDepartment of Government Efficiency\n\n@DOGE\n\n·Follow\n\nGood work by @DeptVetAffairsVA was previously paying \\~$380,000/month for minor website modifications. That contract has not been renewed and the same work is now being executed by 1 internal VA software engineer spending \\~10 hours/week.\n\n4:58 PM · Apr 2, 2025\n\n34.6KReplyCopy link\n\nRead 1.2K replies\n\n---\n\nSubscribe",

      "chunk": "# Post Apocalyptic Computing\n\n12 min read Mar 23, 2025 \n\nSupport this website by purchasing prints of my photographs! Check them out here. \n\nWe live in a world of planned obsolescence. You'd be hard pressed to find a consumer-grade technology manufactured today that will still be working in 10 years. The minimization of circuits is another shame. What used to be repairable by hand is now destined for landfill. The built-in schematics of old have long since given way to soldered RAM and the warranty void stickers of new — if you've torn apart a TV built in the 80s you'll know what I'm talking about.\n\nWhen I first started writing this article in 2023 I had just watched the Silo series on Apple TV (and Severance before that). Silo is a great bit of Sci-Fi, a rare better-than-the-book series, and does an excellent amount of world building. Both Silo and Severance were made with very custom, retro computing machines. In Severance the design is a bit more artificial, nefarious, but in Silo the computers are tools designed to last a couple hundred years. Both shows use computers with CRTs and with mostly character-driven displays.\n\nThe computers in Silo use text heavy UI but display full color and video\n\nThe computers in Silo use text heavy UI but display full color and video\n\nThe computers in Silo really got me thinking about what a computer designed to survive for over a hundred years might look like.\n\nOf course, \"computer\" used to be a very specific term, used for a very small band of machines. Now, many refrigerators could be called a computer. Good luck using a refrigerator to keep a personal diary. The better term, as it applies here, would be general purpose computing machine, which refers to a device where one can largely solve unanticipated problems and, perhaps, even execute code and somehow interface with the outside world.\n\nThere's a certain \"Turing Completeness\" (not in the literal sense — all computers are Turing Complete) when it comes to an Android phone as compared to an iPhone. For example, say that you're trapped in a room and the only way to get out of the door is to insert a USB drive with a text file on it saying \"open sesame\" (like something out of a Resident Evil game). If you've got a USB-C thumb drive, formatted as FAT32, and an Android phone, well you can pull this off. If you have an iPhone, you're out of luck. It's like, in some way, you're on some adventure, and you come upon a certain problem, and you're stuck. Full Stop.\n\nThe ideas as described in this document are attempts to define some sort of device that is \"Turing Complete\" enough to get around as many of these \"full stop\" situations as possible. Back to the Android example, if your thumb drive is USB-A, or is formatted as ExFAT, or if you don't have a text editor installed, then you have hit a full stop.\n\nWhat is this fascination with any of this? I suspect it comes from being born in the 80s, at a time when computers were new and magical. A tool that could solve all problems. And then decades of Star Trek and space survival movies came out. Movies where the lowly hacker walks up to the fortress, jacks into the serial port, and lets himself in. Robocop, Terminator 2, etc.\n\nJohn Connor hacks an ATM in Terminator 2 using a 1989 Atari Portfolio\n\nJohn Connor hacks an ATM in Terminator 2 using a 1989 Atari Portfolio\n\nAnother issue with many modern devices is their requirement for internet access. When I was in high school, sometime in the early 00s, a programmer whom I was job-shadowing with lamented the cycle of computers forever alternating between thin and thick clients. A thin client is a machine that's just a simple keyboard and display that depends on a remote server to function, while a thick client is something like a laptop running Linux or Windows XP. In a way we're now transitioning back towards thin clients. Just look at the Windows 11 OS which has issues during install without internet connectivity. Or even the Adobe software empire which now requires subscriptions to the online Creative Cloud service. Modern computing involves software hamstrung with subscriptions.\n\n_Note that the computers in Silo were technically thin clients. But they didn't have to be!_\n\nMost of these issues stem from corporations trying to wring out every dime they can from consumers. But I'm sure with things like the right to repair movement, and an eventual crash in the technology investment markets, that we'll eventually return to a time where thick clients reign supreme. Companies like Framework are even helping to make repairability a consumer-desirable feature.\n\nBut I digress. What might a general purpose computing machine look like, one that's designed to last over a hundred years, one that would even be useful in some sort of post apocalyptic environment?\n\nWell, such machines obviously need to work without internet access. This might immediately discard modern versions of Windows. macOS is slightly better in this regard. While the OS installer has plenty of hidden surprises, in my experience, it always at least succeeds with an install even without internet access. macOS also doesn't complain about licensing and serial numbers, though it will absolutely complain about running on non-genuine Apple hardware. It's possible to slap together a Hackintosh in some situations, but as the name implies, it's a hack. Apple has always balked at standards, e.g. the new Mac Studio uses proprietary removable storage, so good luck swapping that out in a hundred years.\n\nIt's also important that a computer contain all of the tools necessary to modify its own software, software to replicate itself to other computers, and software to help repair itself or other computers in the case of a catastrophic event. A hundred years is a long time and there will be unanticipated problems along the way. Classes of bugs like the Y2K problem. The need to reduce the OS's strain on battery usage. The need to write new hardware drivers. Rebuilding a kernel is a must.\n\nWhile a Windows or macOS computer _could_ ship with the entire repository and tooling required to build the OS, something only available to Microsoft and Apple employees today, I suspect such repositories would span multiple terabytes and be largely impractical. Plus I guarantee one would need several versions of Visual Studio or Xcode or various runtime versions to build the entirety of Windows or macOS.\n\nLinux and BSD machines have famously made it easy to recompile and install new kernels locally. Some Linux distributions _only_ ship source code and require all binaries to be compiled locally. And while Linux and BSD are great candidate operating systems for the post apocalyptic computer, they aren't necessarily the best choice, but more on that later.\n\nPortability is probably another desirable aspect of such computers. If people migrate around in 100 years then they'll need portable computers. If people don't migrate, well, they can keep a portable computer in the same place for a long time. So massive stationary computers might not be the best 100 year computer. I suppose I could call my 24 year old fully functional iMac G3 a portable computer.\n\nThe iMac G3: Back when Apple made good computers\n\nThe iMac G3: Back when Apple made good computers\n\nNations rise and fall and standards change. It's not guaranteed that a power grid supplying alternating current at 60Hz will be in our future. For that reason the post apocalyptic computer should be able to accept power from a variety of inputs, and accept a wide range of voltage and unregulated currents. Such a machine would need some sort of battery, a circuit to smooth out bumpy electricity, and a pair of alligator clips that works with unanticipated power sources.\n\nA battery is probably the biggest nightmare. It would need to be something that doesn't degrade too quickly. It would also need to be re-creatable in the future once failure inevitably happens. The now banned mercury oxide batteries that powered many 70s era cameras still don't have a perfect replacement after all. The ability to charge a computer using solar panels would certainly be convenient.\n\nThe MNT Reform uses standard 18650 Lithium Ion batteries\n\nThe MNT Reform uses standard 18650 Lithium Ion batteries\n\nThe computer would also need to come with ample documentation, both in print and digital. Documentation that is in print is important for failure scenarios, like when the device doesn't boot. An explanation of how the battery works. An explanation of how the power inputs work. Any instructions on bypassing a dead battery. How to turn the computer on, what sort of sensors it has, how to recover from a failed boot partition, etc., is all required to be in print. Bootstrap stuff.\n\nDigital documentation is needed for everything else. Manuals for programming. How to build the kernel. How to debug rare boot problems for a second computer. How to network with other devices. How to use all of the sensors. How the LCD is attached to the bezel. How to build replacement components or even a new computer from scratch using entirely commodity parts.\n\nIn so many Sci-Fi series, like Star Trek or Silo, it's important for a community to be self-sufficient. For example, producing food, recycling waste, etc. This includes repairs. Can you imagine what Star Trek would look like if they couldn't leave the ship to repair it from the outside? Or how long would a Silo last if one couldn't fix things? Computers are a bit more constrained than a starship, but ideally, if a non-vital component breaks, one could ideally remove it and work on it while reading repair docs from the functioning computer.\n\nThe software on these computers would be extensive as well. A wide array of programming language compilers: C, C++, Rust, etc. Scripting languages as well: Bash and Python both come to mind. Each of these require a compiler/interpreter, programming manuals, and all source code for the compilers and interpreters.\n\nAny software included on the machine should have the source code to build it. Every single aspect of the computer should be reconfigurable. When the computer generates some sort of media to install itself on other computers, such as by creating USB boot drives, it should be able to replicate the current state of the packages as they run on the computer. Assuming the possessor of the computer has made improvements to the software it would be a shame to lose them upon replication.\n\nThe computers also need the ability to rollback the system to a known good state. This can be achieved by using a recovery partition, but it would seem impractical to keep such a partition up to date with improvements made to the system along the way. Something like ZFS snapshots might be more practical. Experiment with changes, improve the system, in case of catastrophe you roll back, in case of success you commit a new filesystem snapshot.\n\nBit-rot is a phenomenon where individual bits of data held in long term storage can become corrupted over time. This is often attributed to cosmic rays but really anything that physically exists will have small changes randomly made to its atoms. For this reason the storage of the computer would probably need to remain largely uncompressed. Errors in uncompressed data are easier to recover from.\n\nSecurity is another awkward concept. Some forms of encryption can result in massive failures in the case of bit-rot. Full disk encryption also makes it difficult to restore a computer in a disaster scenario. I'm not dying on this hill but a hundred year computer doesn't use full disk encryption. When it comes to longevity, a computer will likely change hands many times. It's then questionable whether user authentication is relevant. Or, put another way, is it okay if the security mechanism is that you've locked the computer in a box instead of locking it with a login prompt?\n\nPhysical moving parts are often the first components of a computer to fail. Spinning drives therefore aren't the best storage medium. Hinged displays, like with modern laptops, are another point of failure. Having a machine with a stationary display may be the most resilient.\n\nThe DevTerm doesn't have a hinge. It's a shame the keyboard is so bad.\n\nThe DevTerm doesn't have a hinge. It's a shame the keyboard is so bad.\n\nBefore discussing user interface I'd like to take a quick step back. Computers from decades past largely had text based interfaces. If you're old enough, or a computer programmer, you've seen your fair share of full screen text interfaces. Computers were slow too, of course, so while text interfaces were the standard it's not like those machines were fast enough to draw complex graphics anyway.\n\nFast forward a few decades and computers are now exponentially more powerful than they used to be. They can do all sorts of fancy user interface magic, such as transparent window shadows and glossy window backgrounds which blur the layers behind them which can be overlaid on top of something else in another window that's animated and rendering text. Most of the CPU power of modern machines is squandered to ensure that overcomplicated UI elements with subtle shading and rounded rectangles render at a quick enough pace.\n\nAt the end of the day we don't actually need these crazy complicated user interfaces. I'd argue that for 90% of the most common user actions the Windows 98 UI is better than the Windows 11 UI. In fact old operating systems often draw updates to the screen with less latency than newer operating systems. Over time we've added so many layers of software abstraction that it's resulted in large binaries that consume astronomical amounts of disk space and memory and come with poor performance. Check out Software disenchantment for a nice rant about how software has gotten slow and sloppy.\n\nWindows 98: Back when a start menu was a start menu\n\nWindows 98: Back when a start menu was a start menu\n\nAll this to say that we can do fine with less CPU and memory resources than we have today. The hundred year computer could be served with either a simple graphical user interface or with a text interface.\n\nGoing way back to the Turing Completeness of a computer, in particular regarding how it interacts with the world, it's important that such devices can communicate and consume information about the world over many mediums. What's the ultimate device from Sci-Fi for doing this sort of thing? Why, the humble Star Trek Tricorder of course! While it's fiction there is certainly a lot we can take for inspiration.\n\nThings like Bluetooth and WiFi are useful in today's world, but these complex protocols will likely be extinct in the future. Other forms of radio are certainly going to be more universally beneficial. The post apocalyptic computer will definitely need Software Defined Radio (SDR), which is a hardware radio that can have its properties changed by software. Using something like an RTL-SDR dongle I can listen to AM and RM radio, CB radio, and plenty of folks using amateur radio, though it sadly doesn't allow for transmission. Of course, there is more feature-packed SDR hardware out there, and while the SDR devices of today need to abide by FCC transmission rules, those same rules won't apply in a post apocalyptic scenario (or will at least change over the next 100 years).\n\nThe computer needs speakers. It should probably also have a 15mm audio jack. Other communication devices and sensors would be beneficial: infrared RX / TX, audio RX (mic), visual light RX (camera), Geiger counter. Older ports like serial and parallel are going to be easier to develop with than, say, USB. Powering the device with a traditional power source would be better served with a barrel jack than today's USB-C standard. GPIO ports would also be useful for breadboard development. Having a breadboard built in might be even better.\n\nWhen it comes to keyboards, every key needs to be labeled. Blank keycaps are a definite no-go. Nobody is going to know what those keys do in the future. Having dedicated number keys and F1-F12 keys are ideal, but if a Fn key is required, then the modifier keys should all have proper colored labels. Any key mapping should be done at a hardware level, not software, to ensure key purpose remains consistent. If pressing Fn+3 sends an F3 while booted into the Operating System then it should also send an F3 in the BIOS.\n\nThe ZX Spectrum keyboard: What modifier key is pressed to activate the green functions?\n\nThe ZX Spectrum keyboard: What modifier key is pressed to activate the green functions?\n\nAs far as CPUs go, the x86 architecture has probably run its course, especially with power consumption. You never know what sort of energy crisis may be waiting for us down the road. ARM is interesting from a lower power consumption perspective. RISC-V is interesting from an open source and ability to procure schematics perspective. However, even simpler architectures might be better if a simpler operating system is chosen.\n\nOperating System choice has many effects on such a computer. I believe it comes down to the question of if the OS should be complex, like a BSD or Linux, or simple. A complex OS comes with complexity of maintenance. A computer won't last for a century if some misconfigured service fills the disk with logs. Such a complex kernel can be hard to reason about and make changes to. The distance from kernel code to driver code can also make things hard to grok. Power consumption is going to be higher. It is \"overkill\" if the post apocalyptic computer only needs 1% of the functionality provided by the OS. Overkill translates into failure points.\n\nSimpler operating systems get a bit more interesting. There is actually a purpose built OS that relates to a lot of the ideas I've mentioned in here: DuskOS and CollapseOS. While geared towards the collapse of society (aka post apocalyptic), they're also interesting in that they're built around the Forth language. This is reminiscent of old DOS era computers like the TRS-80 which made it very easy to write and run BASIC programs.\n\n---\n\nIn a world increasingly dominated by planned obsolescence and disposable technology, the idea of a general-purpose computing machine designed to last a century feels both radical and necessary. Drawing inspiration from Sci-Fi, retro computing, and a deep frustration with modern constraints, we can imagine a machine that prioritizes repairability, self-containment, and the ability to modify and replicate itself.\n\nSuch a computer would embrace simplicity over excess, durability over convenience, and openness over restriction. It would rely on robust commodity hardware, energy efficiency, and a software ecosystem without proprietary constraints. The challenges of power sources, bit-rot, and simplified communication protocols all need thoughtful solutions, but the goal remains the same: a machine that endures, adapts, and continues to function even in the face of technological, economic, or societal collapse.\n\nWhether this vision takes form as a movement, a niche project, or a future necessity, the idea remains compelling. As technology continues to cycle between openness and controlled, thick and thin clients, repairability and disposability, we may yet see a return to computing that values longevity and resilience over profit-driven impermanence. The hundred-year computer isn't just a dream — it’s a challenge to rethink the way we build and use technology in an uncertain future.\n\n## Interesting Hardware\n\n* TRS-80 Model 100\n* Cyberdeck\n* MNT Reform\n* RTL-SDR\n* Meshtastic\n* Flipper Zero\n* One Laptop per Child\n\n## Further Reading\n\n* Lockdown: The coming war on general-purpose computing by Cory Doctorow\n* Nikitonsky and the Software Disenchantment\n\nDiscussion: \n\n**Lobsters** lobste.rs **Hacker News** news.ycombinator.com **Tildes** \\~comp **Reddit** /r/programming \n\n Tags:#hardware #decentralization #linux #ewaste \n\nThomas Hunter II Avatar \n\nThomas has contributed to dozens of enterprise Node.js services and has worked for a company dedicated to securing Node.js. He has spoken at several conferences on Node.js and JavaScript and is an O'Reilly published author.\n\nThomas Hunter II Avatar \n\n### Thomas Hunter II\n\n#### @tlhunter\n\nI came here to kick ass, build web applications, and chew bubble gum.
