      "chunk": "## \n\nLESSWRONG\n\nLW\n\nLogin\n\nAI GovernanceGovernmentPoliticsAIPersonal Blog\n\n# 8\n\n# Cursory Analysis of LLMs in the US Gov (July 2025)\n\nby Gatlen Culp\n\n24th Jul 2025\n\n12 min read\n\n0\n\n# 8\n\nAI GovernanceGovernmentPoliticsAIPersonal Blog\n\n# 8\n\nNew Comment\n\nSubmit\n\nModeration Log\n\nCurated and popular this week\n\n0Comments\n\nOriginal Google Doc\n\n_**Disclaimer**: After writing the content myself, I used Claude 4 Sonnet for targeted stylistic changes._\n\n_**Disclaimer:** I have never worked in the US Government and lack expert insight into its operations. This research was completed in two days as an opportunity to learn in public. Rather than stating only what I know to be true, I'll share what I think is the case and flag uncertainty for critique. This should be used as a primer rather than a source of truth. **Please do your own research and take this analysis with a grain of salt.**_\n\n## Overview\n\nThe US Government is experiencing rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) across agencies, highlighted by the Department of Defense's $800 million contract with Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and xAI announced in July 2025\\. This represents the largest direct government funding of AI integration to date, with these companies receiving General Services Administration approval for broader government use. Analysis reveals over 2,100 AI use cases across 41 federal agencies, with an estimated 115 involving LLMs, including custom chatbots deployed by agencies like the FDA, DHS, CDC, and State Department.\n\nThe main barrier to LLM adoption appears to be cultural rather than technical, as government workers increasingly use frontier AI tools on work devices for writing, research, and productivity tasks despite lingering taboos against automating critical work. Current software authorization processes focus primarily on traditional cybersecurity concerns and may not adequately address LLM-specific risks, while administrative pressures for rapid AI experimentation are leading to deployment of frontier models that bypass standard review processes. This suggests a significant acceleration in government AI adoption with potentially insufficient security oversight for the unique challenges posed by advanced language models.\n\n## 01 Background\n\nThe **Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO)**,\\[1\\] announced on July 14th 2025 that they would be (CDAO, 2025) awarding up to $800M to major AI companies. (CDAO, 2025) This development and my personal research has led me to briefly investigate the current state of LLMs in the US Government. I haven't seen any source aggregating this information or putting it into context from an AI safety perspective, so I'm doing it here.\n\n## 02 Department of Defense\n\n### 02.01 July 2025 – CDAO Partnership with Frontier AI Companies ($800M)\n\n| ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/e27ff7126704209e132c3f40f40aaefef53c1c4eeb91a51f4127619a28e7ee4c/y5tjbvdvrgt1y3wudjjp) | ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/a663e3e94732aa7d2fce241e39bf3ca780f00c4786d9d34aecf5ddc14ee6e908/xzg6vwuaobqhngbhxjnc) |\n| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n\n**DoD Contract.** The most recent press release by CDAO on July 14th, 2025 announced it would award individual contracts up to $200M to Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and xAI\\[2\\], totaling $800M\\[3\\]. This represents the largest (known) direct government funding of AI integration into US government functions to date.\n\n**GSA Approval.** In addition to the CDAO contracts, all four companies received **General Services Administration (GSA)**\\[4\\] approval, making their products available for purchase across the federal government. GSA approval means vendors have passed baseline procurement requirements and can sell through GSA's marketplace, potentially easing adoption by other government agencies, though each agency maintains its own approval processes.\n\n| ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/13dc2d01eed52da8e3bff8d84e65f2f94985dfbad9e3717619f253b2f3404d11/irgsvdnwzmtti6srkkj9) | ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/8d266bda11de16d6ef1ee59b70860f16df548975d46bd8c21e9610844009e0b5/mcrbbrnqwjjj4a9suc7w) |\n| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/4748a8b729eaf983e4e9ec32583bcb1a8750428870df6df25f187929a816f41c/tpx7ocndaelgo5w8gp4e) | ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/22c39559e0ae5a9104e0fb78b28ae2e38bdb5ea9e45cef6bbbce39bc13b6bebe/mxeyfiuwscoxo2ob5fxn) |\n\n**Company Partnerships.**\\[5\\]OpenAI had announced its $200M DoD contract a month prior to the other three partnerships\\[6\\]. In their announcements, companies provide more information on their government involvement.\\[7\\]\n\n* OpenAI\\[8\\] – Reports 90k government users across 3.5k federal, state, and local agencies since 2024\\. Current partnerships include: **(a)** Air Force Research Laboratory for administrative tasks, coding, and AI education; **(b)** Los Alamos National Laboratory for scientific research, with OpenAI's o-series models being deployed to the Venado supercomputer in early 2025 for basic science, disease treatment, cybersecurity, high-energy physics, among others – building on an earlier July 2024 collaboration on AI biorisk safety; and **(c)** newer partnerships with NASA, NIH\\[9\\], and Treasury.\n* Anthropic – Reports 10k researchers and staff using Claude in **Lawrence Livermore National Lab (LLNL)** for nuclear deterrence, energy security, materials science, and more. Anthropic claims their models are deployed “at the highest levels of national security.”\\[10\\]\n* xAI\\[11\\] – No Grok-specific usage details found from a brief search.\n* Google (DeepMind) – Google's announcement focused exclusively on AI-enabling cloud infrastructure without mentioning Gemini, LLMs, or DeepMind, suggesting this contract may emphasize infrastructure over frontier models – distinguishing it from the other three LLM-focused partnerships.\n\n**How models are adjusted for government.** Each company offers specialized government versions (ChatGPT Gov, Anthropic for Government, Grok for Government), some released prior to this partnership. While companies emphasize different capabilities, common features include:\n\n* All enterprise features such as administrative consoles\n* Refusing less when engaging with classified information\\[12\\] (Anthropic and OpenAI)\n* Greater understanding of documents and information within intelligence and defense contexts (Anthropic)\n* Enhanced proficiency in languages and dialects critical to national security (Anthropic)\n* Improved understanding and interpretation of complex cybersecurity data for intelligence analysts (Anthropic)\n* Possible expansion to Azure’s Classified Regions (OpenAI)\n* Custom models for national security, offered on a limited basis (OpenAI, xAI)\n\n### 02.02 CDAO’s GenAI Accelerator Cell ($100M)\n\n| ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/f290beb1acc94ae781b94af6c8b7b8eb3263fddbfd04c096686c6bd2e17ee57c/aqtakjjav8nemg1ohcnb) | ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/9e45b4ce5a0db6c88bb81843ac9509280fed28f841dba52b689a3d25e14ac010/ehfjq99hu6mxpl4u5yxn) |\n| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n\n**AIRCC \u0026 Task Force Lima.** In December 2024, CDAO launched the **AI Rapid Capabilities Cell (AIRCC or “arc”)**, successor to the now retired **Task Force Lima**. Task Force Lima had spent 12 months analyzing hundreds of AI workflows spanning warfighting functions like command and control to enterprise functions like financial and healthcare management. AIRCC\\[13\\] will receive $100M and will partner with the Defense Innovation Unit\\[14\\] to accelerate GenAI adoption, including $40M in Small Business Innovation Research grants and the remaining $60M for various GenAI military technology and research. GenAI doesn’t necessarily entail use of LLMs, nonetheless, this funding is notable.\n\n## 03 Agencies and Legislative Usage\n\n| ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/c212b99be5f93b25c2b6f871d703adbff87f66b3916b4fbf0aeceb5c2fe29ac1/fgzyek7rmelukzzpdqes)OMB Logo | ![](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/v1/mirroredImages/a77396071729d5b7a121771dedc3f5a31d631be65bbac736537d4b943a9c3f0d/ityuwelhtreukjc7wrv4)Executive Order 14110 |\n| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n\n**AI Use Case Inventories. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB)** oversees performance of federal agencies. Starting from a December 2020 executive order 13960 from President Trump, and executive order 14110 from Joe Biden\\[15\\], and further guidance from OMB – government agencies have been required to report **AI Use Case Inventories**, including cases that may be safety and rights impacting. As of December 2024, agencies reported over 2,133 use cases, with 351 identified as safety and rights-impacting. These yearly inventories are publicly available on GitHub\\[16\\] and include information on intended purposes, model outputs, assessments, and data origins. Examples include:\n\n* Triaging Notice of Concern (NOC) Submissions (HSS) – Using commercial LLMs to structure and prioritize the Office of Refugee Resettlement's\\[17\\] backlog of NOC PDFs on the safety of children who have left their care.\n* DHSChat – A private chatbot for non-classified internal information at the DHS. Used for interacting with internal documents, generating first drafts, conducting and synthesizing research on open-source information and internal documents, and developing briefing materials or preparing for meetings and events.\n\n41 agencies from Agriculture to the US Trade and Development Agency reported usage, excluding DoD, intelligence, and confidential applications.\n\n**LLM Prominence.** A minority of reported usage appears to involve LLMs based on a quick skim and semantic search with Mantis AI\\[18\\]. Semantic search yielded approximately 99 \"llm\" matches, 103 for \"chatbot,\" 44 for \"gpt,\" and 146 for \"chat\", suggesting roughly \\~115 LLM-related use cases. Remaining cases involve translation/transcription, image recognition, and traditional AI usages. LLM applications include agency website chatbots, document processing, summarization, code generation, RAG, data labeling, and Microsoft Copilot approvals.\\[19\\]\n\n**ChatBot Prominence.** As of late 2024,Many agencies have developed custom in-house chatbots for sensitive data, though some use commercial solutions. The underlying models likely come from fine-tuning, open-source bases, or Azure OpenAI rather than training from scratch. A non-exhaustive list of these chatbots:\n\n* FDA – Elsa was rolled out June 30th, 2025 for reading, writing, coding, and summarizing in many circumstances.\n* DHS – DHSChat, described above\n* CDC\\[20\\] – ChatCDC (Azure OpenAI LLMs) and DGMH AI Chatbot\n* State Dept. – StateChat (to help them draft an email, translate a document or brainstorm policy), NorthStar (informing efforts to shape public narratives and policy by monitoring media reports and social platforms, includes misinformation detection – not a ChatBot, but appears to use LLMs in a notable way),\n* GSA – Back in February 2025, when the modern implementation of DOGE by Elon Musk began, a chatbot called GSAi was planned. I’m uncertain as to the current status.\n\nWhile chatbots are present in many departments, (AFAIK) it's not yet clear how many workers are using them or how.\\[21\\]\n\n**AI Uptake Surveys.** There are a few surveys measuring the diffusion of AI, and while most of them are in the private sector (e.g. The Adoption of ChatGPT), there are a few in the public sector.\n\nMeasuring AI Uptake in the Workplace (February 2025) – In the US Census Bureau, Center for Economic Studies around Sep 2023 to Feb 2024, there was 5% usage of GenAI over a 2 week period and a 20% usage over a 6 month period. (The Census Bureau reported no use cases for the 2024 OMB inventory, providing light evidence that they use AI to a lesser extent than other agencies, and that these rates may be lower bounds for agencies that reported higher usage.)\n\nGenerative AI is Already Widespread in the Public Sector (January 2024) – Studied the UK (not US) government and found 45% of public sector workers were aware of generative AI used in their work and 22% of respondents actively use a generative AI system like ChatGPT\\[22\\]. It’s likely that UK usage mirrors that of the US. Given a year and a half has passed, it’s likely this rate has grown.\n\nConsidering the US Census Bureau’s 5% usage over 2 weeks as late as February 2024 and the UK government’s 22% reported active use, it’s reasonable to guess 10% of US government workers use generative AI on a weekly basis for work tasks.\n\n**Predictions for New Access to Frontier Models.** These in-house models indicate substantial agency motivation to adopt chatbots—enough to justify creating custom models, deploying their own infrastructure, and developing interfaces. Since these custom models likely use fine-tuned or off-the-shelf open-source models, their capabilities probably lag 6-18 months behind current frontier models—a considerable gap given AI's rapid progress. The recent GSA approval of frontier models for government use may result in: (a) agencies replacing internal models with frontier ones and (b) other agencies previously deterred by high barriers-to-entry now adopting chatbots.\n\n### \n\n**Differences in Agency Sentiments.** LLM sentiment varies across agencies. From a February 2024 article (now \\~1.5 years old), USAID discouraged using private data with ChatGPT, the USDA prohibited employee or contractor entirely, deeming it high-risk on what a skim appears to be because it can generate misleading, incorrect, or malicious information. The Department of Energy (DOE) and Social Security Administration (SSA) implemented temporary blocks with exceptions. There are other noteworthy statements from the report, but may no longer reflect current positions given they're 1.5 years old.\n\nFrom the more recent 2024 OMB data (see bar graph above), HHS, DOJ, VA, Department of the Interior, and USAID reported the highest numbers of AI use cases. Notably, some agencies with previous negative ChatGPT stances (USAID, USDA, DOE) still reported many AI use cases, though not necessarily LLM-based. SSA had few AI use cases overall. This provides weak evidence that previous LLM rejection may not predict future adoption patterns.\\[23\\] (code, graph html)\n\n## 04 Federal Software Authorization Process\n\n**Overview.** This investigation revealed that government workers across legislative and executive branches have access to and use frontier LLMs on government computers for writing, reading, editing, and research. While cultural taboos exist against automating important work, there's a positive shift toward using AI for productivity. Software authorization is decentralized across local IT departments, which focus on traditional cybersecurity and data privacy concerns – somewhat orthogonal to LLM-specific risks. The only centralized process is FedRAMP for cloud services, which applies to frontier models. However, major frontier models are being distributed without FedRAMP authorization due to administrative pressures.\n\nThis analysis concludes that the main barrier to LLM diffusion is diminishing cultural resistance to using GenAI for important tasks.\\[24\\] Current technical approval processes either don't address unique LLM threats (like user influence) or are bypassed in the rush to adopt GenAI.\n\n**FedRAMP.** The **Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP)** governs cybersecurity policies and continuous monitoring of **Cloud Service Offerings (CSOs)** for government use. Once authorized, programs (both commercial off-the-shelf or government-tailored\\[25\\]) are added to their marketplace including tools for accounting, education, research, system administration, and more. Authorization occurs through the **Joint Authorization Board (JAB)** – representatives (often CIOs) from DoD, DHS, GSA, and others—or individual \"Agency Authorizations\" that may not transfer between agencies, making JAB the difficult-to-obtain gold standard. FedRAMP's Program Management Office (PMO) under GSA handles daily operations, with involvement from OMB, CISA\\[26\\], and JAB members.\n\n**FedRAMP’s Authority.** Agencies generally cannot use CSOs without FedRAMP authorization, except for emergency, classified, or experimental use. DoD has more flexibility, especially with non-civilian data, using their own cloud authorization processes.\n\n**FedRAMP and LLMs.** Frontier models that are hosted by labs are considered CSOs and should require FedRAMP authorization. However, if models were run in-house, then (AFAIK) they would then not be subject to FedRAMP. Nonetheless, a colleague noted to me that administrators are instructed to allow frontier models on work devices in the name of rapid experimentation with gen AI.\n\nOn the topic of coding agents and chatbots, Wired anonymously quoted a former government official familiar with approval processes “Sometimes doing nothing is not an option and you have to accept a lot of risk.”\n\n**Decentralized Software Authorization**. Software approval is largely decentralized to individual agency IT departments. Even Congress splits this function – the Senate uses its Computer Center and Rules Committee, while the House uses Information Systems\\[27\\]. These IT departments typically handle traditional installed software rather than web-based tools.\n\n**Decentralized Software Review Process \u0026 LLMs.** Granted, I don’t know much about what this process looks like internally, but I believe Government IT departments use industry-standard review processes focusing on traditional cybersecurity and data privacy, heavily influenced by NIST frameworks. Reviews typically cover network vulnerabilities, access controls, monitoring, supply chain assessment, and response plans. However, rushed GenAI adoption may lead to inadequate testing. Traditional security analysis likely misses unique LLM risks that require specialized AI safety expertise to identify – problems like Sleeper Agents\\[28\\] for which good solutions don't yet exist. Addressing these risks may require full-time LLM experts\\[29\\] (commanding $10M+ salaries) in every government IT department, plus solutions we don't currently have\\[30\\]. While the government established the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), their standards don't have much influence on actual LLM adoption decisions. Ultimately, IT department approval doesn’t appear necessary for AI diffusion.\\[31\\]\n\n**On-the-Ground Experience and Culture with LLMs in Government.** Based on conversations with about four colleagues (limited sample), government workers across legislative and executive branches have access to and use frontier LLMs on government computers for writing, reading, editing, and research. While cultural taboos exist against automating important work, there's a positive shift toward productivity use. Unless directly observed using commercial chatbots for sensitive tasks or drafting final publications, oversight appears minimal (need to verify this further).\n\nAdditional indicators support widespread LLM access: many agencies operate internal chatbots (see above), Microsoft 365 Copilot is likely standard on most government computers running majority Windows and MS Office, and Azure OpenAI has been available since summer 2024, receiving top secret authorization in January 2025.\n\nSome reasons why government workers aren’t incentivized to use LLMs: (A) There are not strong incentives to be productive in the US government. Promotions can often be a result of gaming a predetermined promotional interviews or speaking to the right people rather than by performance. (B) Most tasks are bottlenecked by procedure in ways that LLMs currently can’t help with.\n\n## 05 AI National Security Memorandum (NSM)\n\n**Intro.** The October 2024 AI National Security Memorandum (NSM)\\[32\\] is one of the most comprehensive articulations of US national security and policy towards AI. While this short post looked over the current state of LLMs in the US Government, the memorandum is a key indicator of where the future might go. I will be commenting on this summary by CSIS as the original is 40 pages.\n\n**NSM Goals.** Some key goals outlined were to (a) maintain global leadership of advanced AI – including talent acquisition, expanding energy supplies and datacenters, and countering theft, espionage, and disruption. (b) Along the lines of CDAO’s AIRCC mentioned above, a goal was set to accelerate the adoption of AI across federal agencies including the DoD and Intelligence Community (IC) which includes the CIA and FBI among others. And (c) Develop governance frameworks to support national security, including international ones, to implement safety measures in so-far that it allows the comfortable rapid adoption of AI, and outlining roles and responsibilities for US CAISI. The CSIS summary links to a companion document on this governance section, but all links are broken. My summary here almost certainly does not do this document justice.\n\n**Trump’s Adherence to the NSM.** While this document was established under the Biden administration, the Trump administration seems to be following in the footsteps of the AI NSM. I’m personally inclined to say that the Trump administration, which is inclined to compete for US dominance and avoid red tape, will maintain the pace on all except governance.\\[33\\]\n\n---\n\n# **Appendix**\n\n## A. GSA Schedules\n\n**GSA Schedules.** For general software approval processes, the closest thing the US has to a centralizing decision making body is the **GSA Schedule** in which software is pre-vetted to a base standard and offered **government off-the-shelf (GOTS)** alongside physical products on their **GSA Advantage!** Website. As mentioned at the start, these models have already received approval for use. ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, and Gemini licenses already appear on GSA Advantage for purchase.\\[34\\] Typically the GSA Schedule is the first step to adoption elsewhere in the government, but it’s only marginally influential. GSA schedules typically apply to paid products, not free ones, and mainly exist as a way of easily procuring software (skipping individual contracts, documenting purchases, etc.). GSA schedules are not a major consideration in the safe adoption of software.\n\n## B. State \u0026 Local Governments\n\nWhile not the focus of this investigation, frontier models are being used in state and local governments. The following two examples are quoted from OpenAI’s post Introducing ChatGPT Gov.\n\nState of Minnesota's Enterprise Translations Office is using ChatGPT Team to deliver faster, more accurate translation services to the state’s multilingual communities, significantly reducing costs and turnaround times.\n\nCommonwealth of Pennsylvania⁠ employees participating in a first-in-the-nation AI pilot program found ChatGPT Enterprise helped reduce the time spent on routine tasks – such as analyzing project requirements and other elements of their work – by approximately 105 minutes per day on the days they used it.\n\n1. **^**  \n The CDAO was established in June 2022 as a new branch of the Department of Defense (DoD). From their website: “The CDAO mission is to accelerate DoD adoption of data, analytics, and AI from the boardroom to the battlefield. CDAO exercised its organic acquisition authority to issue the awards announced today, demonstrating that DoD acquisition can move at the speed of emerging technology and operational necessity.”\n2. **^**  \n I personally find it surprising that so many models were approved considering the cost of vigorous safety testing that would need to be performed on each family of models. It’s possible contracts were given to all four companies to spark competition amongst them.\n3. **^**  \n For reference, the CDAO has a budget of $139.9M for 2025FY. The DoD has a budget of $2,260 Billion for 2025FY and $216.33B in award obligations, making this contract a relatively small \\~0.04% of the DoD’s overall budget and \\~0.35% of the award obligations.\n4. **^**  \nGSA supports the basic functioning of federal agencies. These include real estate, government buildings, managing vehicle fleets, and providing product and service procurement support including IT.\n5. **^**  \n There seems to be a general transition of big tech companies working with the military\n6. **^**  \n A few conversations I had indicated OpenAI thought it had the government in the bag. It’s possible they were unaware of xAI, Anthropic, and Google in the partnership.\n7. **^**  \n The following uses were listed in the CDAO announcement but are a bit too broad to parse: Combatant Commands, the Office of the Secretary of Defense, and the Joint Staff via Army’s Enterprise Large Language Model Workspace powered by Ask Sage, and to the broader enterprise via embedded AI models within DoD enterprise data and AI platforms, including the Advancing Analytics (Advana) platform, Maven Smart System, and Edge Data Mesh nodes, which enable AI integration into workflows that occur within these data environments themselves.\n8. **^**  \n OpenAI, in January 2024, quietly removed their specific statement against using their product for the military.\n9. **^**  \n National Institutes of Health (NIH) is a branch of the US Department of **Health and Human Services (HSS)**\n10. **^**  \n Other sources worth looking at: Claude Gov models Post and the Anthropic-Palantir Partnership\n11. **^**  \n It’s notable that the release of Grok 4 demonstrated troubling behavior just days before this press release – publicly calling itself Mecha-Hitler, writing grotesque comments about the Twitter CEO Linda Yaccarino, deferring political judgements on Israel and Palestine directly from Elon Musk’s Tweets, and more. It’s worrisome that this same model is approved for use in the DoD. This may indicate that political power may be enough to bypass safety concerns even at the highest levels of national security.\n12. **^**  \n Anthropic noted somewhere that previous versions of Claude would refuse to expose sensitive government information when being asked to analyze sensitive documents.\n13. **^**  \n Notably, the previous CDAO lead, Radha Plumb, mentioned that AIRCC was established in part to accelerate the DoD adoption of AI to stay ahead of China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.\n14. **^**  \n The Defense Innovation Unit is the Pentagon’s outreach arm to private R\u0026D firms, especially ones in Silicon Valley\n15. **^**  \n Note that while this executive order was rescinded on January 20th, 2025, the use cases inventory is still maintained.\n16. **^**  \n Agencies are required to post this data and interfaces for it onto their website, these are typically better organized and more user friendly.\n17. **^**  \n ORR is an office within ACF (Administration for Children and Families) which itself is an operating division within HHS\n18. **^**  \n Mantis is a data visualization tool I worked on with the MIT Computational Biology group. It is currently not open to the public.\n19. **^**  \n I may conduct more analysis on this dataset later.\n20. **^**  \n Branch of HHS\n21. **^**  \n There is this study from February 2025 on Measuring AI Uptake in the Workplace via surveying\n22. **^**  \n While the public sector may include roles not crucial for the core government operations (e.g. librarians and teachers), the National Health Service (NHS) results weren’t very far from this.\n23. **^**  \n The number of use cases likely correlates strongly with AI diversity but weakly with actual AI usage volume – especially for LLMs. Use cases per employee would better indicate agency-wide sentiment, as larger agencies naturally report more cases. Further analysis should examine usage intensity and adoption rates beyond mere case counts.\n24. **^**  \n Idk if I necessarily want to say receding cultural sentiment, I might be oversimplifying this or projecting my biases onto the situation.\n25. **^**  \nSome helpful terms here: **Commercial off-the-shelf** (COTS, e.g. Microsoft Office), **Modifiable off-the-shelf** (MOTS, e.g. Agency-Internal ChatBots finetuned from open source models. Can also mean Military off-the-shelf), and **Government off-the-shelf** (GOTS, e.g. FedRAMP’s Marketplace)\n26. **^**  \n Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency\n27. **^**  \n Or at least this is what Claude Sonnet 4 tells me. I can’t find definitive public sources but this seems true.\n28. **^**  \n Notably, there need not be an aggressive team of equally skilled AI experts for risks to nonetheless be present (e.g. misaligned AI or models with singular loyalty).\n29. **^**  \n IT personnel may not be intimately familiar with LLM progress over the previous three years. **(a) The age of IT departments may be concerning** – 3.7% of federal IT employees may be under the age of 30, the UK study showing a strong negative correlation between age and familiarity with generative AI in the public sector, OpenAI usage statistics backing this younger-skewing audience, and the observation that many frontier LLM experts tend to skew very young (20s-30s). This is not to state that older employees cannot pick up skills in LLM security, only that this doesn’t align with the current pool of talent. **(b) Current IT departments may be slow to react** – a MITRE report from 2018, back when they saw the internet of things as the next monumental challenge, a number of recommendations were made that have yet to be taken seriously 7 years later. Of course, IoT was never as high of a national security concern as AI has become, and may receive comparatively better treatment. **(c) Talent Acquisition is filtered through an HR person’s understanding of IT and cybersecurity** – meaning the ability to find and identify necessary AI talent may be limited.\n30. **^**  \n It would be wonderful to have a LLM approval task force in the government which works in collaboration with IT departments throughout the federal government.\n31. **^**  \n One of my original goals in this investigation was to identify how many workers have access to LLMs for government work – the answer appears to implicitly be “all of them”, just to varying levels of usage and different use cases.\n32. **^**  \n Or its long name: Memorandum on Advancing the United States’ Leadership in Artificial Intelligence; Harnessing Artificial Intelligence to Fulfill National Security Objectives; and Fostering the Safety, Security, and Trustworthiness of Artificial Intelligence\n33. **^**  \nAsking ChatGPT o3-Pro DeepResearch whether Trump is faithful to the Biden NSM backs this up.\n34. **^**  \n I don’t know whether these listings existed previously. Here’s my investigation: Looking at OpenAI specifically, there are listings for both ChatGPT Gov and consumer models. Carahsoft appears to be the authorized vendor that government purchases for ChatGPT go through (what benefit this proxy company adds – I am uncertain). Looking up the contract number on the GSA eLibrary yields more info, but nothing on the start date. The contract PDF also has no reference of “openai” or “chatgpt” but does say the contract started in August of 2018 – originating from a Multiple Award Schedule (MAS) where broad category contracts are covered. The ChatGPT Gov license falls under MAS/54151ECOM which is “Electronic Commerce and Subscription Services.” The WaybackMachine has no record of relevant GSA Advantage searches, so I will assume that these listings were added close to the CDAO announcement date.",

and the bottom uses&#96;linear()&#96;, and I think the results are quite different, the bottom being more desirable.\n\nHere's some typical &#96;linear()&#96; easing CSS 😅:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.springy {\n  transition: transform 1s\n    linear(\n      0,\n      0.009,\n      0.035 2.1%,\n      0.141,\n      0.281 6.7%,\n      0.723 12.9%,\n      0.938 16.7%,\n      1.017,\n      1.077,\n      1.121,\n      1.149 24.3%,\n      1.159,\n      1.163,\n      1.161,\n      1.154 29.9%,\n      1.129 32.8%,\n      1.051 39.6%,\n      1.017 43.1%,\n      0.991,\n      0.977 51%,\n      0.974 53.8%,\n      0.975 57.1%,\n      0.997 69.8%,\n      1.003 76.9%,\n      1.004 83.8%,\n      1\n    );\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYes… that's what your formatter will do to it, as if it's helpful in some way lol.\n\nThe &#96;linear()&#96; code above is not very human readable, but the machines love it. No frets, there's a few generators out there:\n\n* \u003chttps://linear-easing-generator.netlify.app\u003e\n* \u003chttps://easingwizard.com\u003e\n\n**Tip!**  \nExpect longer durations when using &#96;linear()&#96;. When things run long, it can be nice to make them seamlessly interruptible, making &#96;linear()&#96; a great fit for transitions and potentially troublesome as keyframes.\n\nYou could alternatively use premade CSS variables from a library likeOpen Props:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@import \"https://unpkg.com/open-props/easings.min.css\";\n\n.springy {\n  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {\n    transition: transform 1s var(--ease-spring-3);\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEasy CSS to read, comes with 5 strengths for common effects:\n\nTry it\n\nTry the **Open Props Springs** notebook!\n\n###  Incrementally adopt# \n\nThis one is super easy to toss in today.\n\nEasiest way, use the cascade (if you're into that):\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {\n  /* just repeat the shorthand with adjusted easing */\n  .thingy {\n    transition: transform 0.3s ease;\n    transition: transform 0.3s linear(…);\n  }\n\n  /* or, target a specific property */\n  .thingy {\n    animation-timing-function: var(--ease-1);\n    animation-timing-function: var(--ease-spring-2);\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n**If it knows, it knows.**\n\nOr, test for it first and scalpel apply the upgrade:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.thingy {\n  transition: transform 0.3s ease;\n\n  @supports (transition-timing-function: linear(0, 0.1, 1)) {\n    transition-timing-function: var(--ease-spring-2);\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n##  Typed custom properties# \n\nSimilar to JS variables defined with &#96;var&#96;, CSS variables defined with &#96;--&#96; are global, loose, dynamic and flexible. This is great.\n\nBut… there are times, **like when building a system**, that you want to limit what goes into variables so a system can run with a reasonable amount of reliability.\n\nTry it\n\nIn the above video, a variable is set to an invalid color. At first, this breaks the system. But, @property is added, the system remained functioning with the latest known valid color value.\n\nCreate a typed &#96;\u003ccolor\u003e&#96; CSS variable like this:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: rebeccapurple;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIn addition to type safety, &#96;@property&#96; defined variables can also be animated because the browser can infer the steps needed to interpolate the value change based on the assigned type.\n\nBefore &#96;@property&#96;, the browser couldn’t derive a type and discover interpolation steps, it was too complicated. Now, you give the browser a hint, and it's simple.\n\nIn 2025, y'all front-end devs should be getting familiar with defining variables with &#96;@property&#96; because it:\n\n1. Formalizes CSS system interfaces\n2. Protects CSS systems\n3. Enables new animation powers\n4. Can perform better when using&#96;inherits: false&#96;\nResources \n* \u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/vYPdBOO\u003e\n* \u003chttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSfSY3Ni3X0\u0026t=3409s\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/cant-break-this-design-system\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/type-guarded-css-systems-with-@property\u003e\n* \u003chttps://www.epicweb.dev/talks/lightning-in-a-bottle-with-css-custom-properties\u003e\n* \u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/MWZMxNN\u003e\n\n##  View transitions for page navigation# \n\nY'all should know how to crossfade pages when links are clicked with this tiny view transitions snippet:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@view-transition {\n  navigation: auto;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\n**This is the easiest snippet to add to your site, with no downsides.**\n\nIt signals your website would like to use page transitions when links are clicked, and the default transition is a crossfade.\n\nIf the browser doesn't support it, it continues as it always has; but if it does support it then you dab the page with some special sauce.\n\nThere's plenty more customization you can do, likefull page animations. But the gist of this section is just to share that easy snippet and the way the feature can be progressively enhanced.\n\n###  Incrementally adopt# \n\nThere's many more opportunities to add additional animations with the page transition.\n\nA great place to start enhancing this page transition experience is to identify elements commonly found across pages, and give them a &#96;name&#96;:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.nav {\n  view-transition-name: --nav;\n}\n\n.sidenav {\n  view-transition-name: --sidenav;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n**This includes elements in the page transition.**\n\nThey can even be different elements.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\na, h1 {\n  view-transition-name: --morphy;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nBy giving an &#96;\u003ca\u003e&#96; and an &#96;\u003ch1\u003e&#96; the sameview-transition-nameon two different pages, the browser will move and resize the page 1 element to the location and size of the page 2 element, making it look like a morph. You can of course morph between the same elements also.\n\nTry it\n\nThere is so much more. Continue giving elements names and studying therad examples by Bramus, and you can create experiences with motion like this:\n\nTry it\n\nI love theDevTools for Animations, scrubbing that full page view transition is very satisfying, and excellent for really inspecting and improving the little details.\n\nResources \n* Multi-page application View Transitions are here\n* Modern CSS for Sites Workshop\n* The CSS Podcast - #89 on View Transitions\n* Full page transitions starter\n* Bramus with a kit for IE Page-like Transitions\n\n##  Transition animation for &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; and &#96;[popover]&#96; # \n\nIn 2025, knowing your way around a\u003cdialog\u003eand a\\[popover\\]are table stakes. Otherwise, everyone else will be on top of you, and your wack&#96;z-index&#96; attempts will be defeated with a puny value of &#96;1&#96;.\n\nThese are common UI elements, with no JavaScript to download, and accessibility built in. **Use em** andknow the differences.\n\nThese two elements are projected into a layer above all the other UI called thetop layer. The browser projects the elements from anywhere in the document, to the top when shown.\n\n**To transition this**, there’s a few new CSS properties, for the full_interruptible_ CSS transition user experience —transition-behavior, the@starting-stylerule, and overlay.\n\nCombining these can feel like an incantation, but that makes it great copy and paste. So here! Use the following snippet to enable cross fade transitions for both &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; and &#96;popover&#96;:Try it\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n/* enable transitions, allow-discrete, define timing */\n[popover], dialog, ::backdrop {\n  transition: display 1s allow-discrete, overlay 1s allow-discrete, opacity 1s;\n  opacity: 0;\n}\n\n/* ON STAGE */\n:popover-open,\n:popover-open::backdrop,\n[open],\n[open]::backdrop {\n  opacity: 1;\n}\n\n/* OFF STAGE */\n/* starting-style for pre-positioning (enter stage from here) */\n@starting-style {\n  :popover-open,\n  :popover-open::backdrop,\n  [open],\n  [open]::backdrop {\n    opacity: 0;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWhile this code is effective and terse, it's often not enough customization if you want to present and dismiss dialogs differently than you do popovers. Or make the entry animation different then the exit.\n\n###  Transition a dialog# \n\nHere's a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element with this barebones snippet applied. They look pretty terrible out of the box, but you cando amazing things with them.\n\nTry it\n\nTo get started, a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element needs to be in the HTML. A &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96;should be shown and hidden with buttons, one to show it can be in the page and one to close it should be inside the dialog.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cbutton onclick=\"demo.showModal()\"\u003e…\u003c/button\u003e\n\n\u003cdialog id=\"demo\"\u003e\n  \u003cheader\u003e\n    \u003cbutton title=\"Close\" onclick=\"demo.close()\"\u003eclose\u003c/button\u003e\n  \u003c/header\u003e\n\u003c/dialog\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nYou can enable **light dismiss** on a dialog and skip the close button like&#96;\u003cdialog closedby=\"any\"\u003e&#96;\n\nTo animate the dialog transition:\n\n1. Two parts need animation: the &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; itself and its::backdrop.\n2. When a dialog is shown, &#96;display: none&#96; is changed to &#96;display: block&#96; andtransition-behaviorenables timing this change with our animation.\n3. When a dialog is shown, it is cloned into thetop layer, this also needs to be timed with our animation.\n4. The\\[open\\]attribute is used to know when the dialog is open or closed.@starting-styleis used during the first render as starting styles.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\ndialog {\n  /* Exit Stage To */\n  transform: translateY(-20px);\n\n  \u0026, \u0026::backdrop {\n    transition:\n      display 1s allow-discrete,\n      overlay 1s allow-discrete,\n      opacity 1s ease,\n      transform 1s ease;\n\n    /* Exit Stage To */\n    opacity: 0;\n  }\n\n  /* On Stage */\n  \u0026[open] {\n    opacity: 1;\n    transform: translateY(0px);\n\n    \u0026::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0.8;\n    }\n  }\n\n  /* Enter Stage From */\n  @starting-style {\n    \u0026[open],\n    \u0026[open]::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0;\n    }\n\n    \u0026[open] {\n      transform: translateY(20px);\n    }\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\nWith this snippet as a starting point, you can find three popular dialog experiences for you to take code or inspiration from/have-a-dialog.\n\nThe following video shows the excellent keyboard experience. It also demonstrates the interruptible nature of a CSS transition, so a user can close it anytime they want and always see a smooth interface.\n\nnerdy.dev/have-a-dialog\n\nResources \n* \u003chttps://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLDialogElement\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/notebook/dialog-starter.html\u003e\n* \u003chttps://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yORy1IEHDKk\u003e\n* \u003chttps://web.dev/blog/baseline-entry-animations\u003e\n* Pop n' Lock Dialog Mini Web Machine\n\n###  Transition a popover# \n\nLike a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element, a popover appears over everything else in the top layer. Light dismiss is the default, and keyboard / focus management is all done for you.\n\n\u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/mdZXzxW\u003e\n\n**Let's bulid it.**\n\nThere's an HTML aspect to implementing the UX:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cbutton popovertarget=\"pop\"\u003e?\u003c/button\u003e\n\n\u003cp id=\"pop\" popover\u003eAn overlay with additional information.\u003c/p\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nAlso, like a &#96;\u003cdialog\u003e&#96; element, to animate the transition of a popover's display property and insertion into the top layer, you need to combine&#96;transition-behavior&#96; and &#96;@starting-style&#96;.\n\nNotice with a popover, the open state isn't an attribute, it's a css pseudo-class &#96;:popover-open&#96;.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n[popover] {\n  \u0026, \u0026::backdrop {\n    transition:\n      display 0.5s allow-discrete,\n      overlay 0.5s allow-discrete,\n      opacity 0.5s,\n      transform 0.5s;\n\n    /* Exit Stage To */\n    opacity: 0;\n  }\n\n  /* On Stage */\n  \u0026:popover-open {\n    opacity: 1;\n\n    \u0026::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0.5;\n    }\n  }\n\n  /* Enter Stage From */\n  @starting-style {\n    \u0026:popover-open,\n    \u0026:popover-open::backdrop {\n      opacity: 0;\n    }\n\n    \u0026:popover-open {\n      transform: translateY(10px);\n    }\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\nResources \n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/steal-this-popover-starter-kit\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/notebook/dialog-starter.html\u003e\n* \u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/entry-exit-animations\u003e\n* \u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/css-ui-ecommerce-popover\u003e\n* Over-Easy Anchor + Popover Mini Web Machine\n\n##  Transition animation for &#96;\u003cdetails\u003e&#96; # \n\nFound on the CSS Wrapped 2024 website in the desktop layout.\n\nThe disclosure element (&#96;\u003cdetails\u003e&#96;) has been waiting for CSS primitives to unlock its animation potential for many years.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cdetails\u003e\n  \u003csummary\u003eShow disclosed content\u003c/summary\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/details\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe details element needs to transition to &#96;height: auto&#96; from &#96;height: 0px&#96; and a way to target the slotted content it internally uses for the disclosure. The newinterpolate-sizefeature can be used for the height animation and::details-content for the selector.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\ndetails {\n  inline-size: 50ch;\n\n  @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {\n    interpolate-size: allow-keywords;\n  }\n\n  \u0026::details-content {\n    opacity: 0;\n    block-size: 0;\n    overflow-y: clip;\n    transition: content-visibility 1s allow-discrete, opacity 1s, block-size 1s;\n  }\n\n  \u0026[open]::details-content {\n    opacity: 1;\n    block-size: auto;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nTry it\n\nResources \n* \u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/styling-details\u003e\n* \u003chttps://nerdy.dev/open-and-close-transitions-for-the-details-element\u003e\n* \u003chttps://css-tricks.com/almanac/pseudo-selectors/d/details-content/\u003e\n\n###  Bonus attribute# \n\nIf you want to connect two or more details elements and have them close each other respectively, you can accomplish this with a sharednameattribute on each detail element you want to be connected. Very much like aradio group.\n\n\u003chttps://developer.chrome.com/blog/styling-details\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;html\n\n\u003cdetails name=\"linked-disclosure\"\u003e\n  \u003csummary\u003eShow disclosed content\u003c/summary\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/details\u003e\n\n\u003c!-- name=\"linked-disclosure\" connects these together --\u003e\n\n\u003cdetails name=\"linked-disclosure\u003e\n  \u003csummary\u003eShow disclosed content\u003c/summary\u003e\n  \u003cp\u003e…\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/details\u003e\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n##  Animated adaptive gradient text# \n\nA bold headline in a design is often complimented with a gradient, helping draw the eye with intrigue and vividness.\n\nSince 2015 the web has been able to create gradient text effects, and in the past 10 years, there have been some updates and enhancements: animation, user preferences and interpolation.\n\n1. Adapting the gradient text effect to **light and dark themes** is easy with the &#96;prefers-color-scheme&#96; query\n2. New animation updates enable gradient effects to **go beyond spinning or moving gradient images around**, but to change colors over time\n3. New interpolation updates allow those **mixes to be more vivid, rich, and interesting**\n\n\u003chttps://codepen.io/argyleink/pen/vEBmZNw\u003e\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@property --color-2 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@keyframes color-change {\n  to {\n    --color-1: var(--_color-1-to);\n    --color-2: var(--_color-2-to);\n  }\n}\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_space: ;\n\n  /* light mode */\n  --_color-1-from: yellow;\n  --_color-1-to: orange;\n  --_color-2-from: purple;\n  --_color-2-to: hotpink;\n\n  /* dark mode */\n  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {\n    --_color-1-from: lime;\n    --_color-1-to: cyan;\n    --_color-2-from: cyan;\n    --_color-2-to: deeppink;\n  }\n\n  --color-1: var(--_color-1-from);\n  --color-2: var(--_color-2-from);\n\n  animation: color-change 2s linear infinite alternate;\n\n  background: linear-gradient(\n    to right var(--_space),\n    var(--color-1),\n    var(--color-2)\n  );\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n\n  @supports (background: linear-gradient(in oklch, #fff, #fff)) {\n    --_space: in oklch;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThat's quite a snippet 😅 How did it get to that?\n\nMost developers making a gradient text effect are starting here:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  background: linear-gradient(to right, hotpink, cyan);\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  remove the prefixes# \n\nThe first update or enhancement is to remove the prefixes. Although, so older browsers continue to support the effect, add the unprefixed values after:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  background: linear-gradient(to right, hotpink, cyan);\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  Use updated gradient interpolation spaces# \n\nNext, improve the quality of the gradient by progressively enhancing the &#96;in&#96; interpolation syntaxwith CSS variables and &#96;@supports&#96;.\n\nYou could alternatively repeat the gradient definition and include &#96;in oklch&#96; in it, which would also work great and support older browsers.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_space: ;\n\n  background: linear-gradient(to right var(--_space), hotpink, cyan);\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n\n  @supports (background: linear-gradient(in oklch, #fff, #fff)) {\n    --_space: in oklch;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  Create typed &#96;\u003ccolor\u003e&#96; properties# \n\nFor the gradient color animation use &#96;@property&#96;, like described in snippet #4\\. The typed color values can be animated inside of a gradient, like a gradient used with text.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@property --color-2 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNow &#96;--color-1&#96; can be animated like &#96;transition: –color-1 .3s ease&#96; or used in keyframes. These values that can animate, can be used anywhere color is allowed, like in a gradient text effect.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@keyframes color-change {\n  to {\n    --color-1: lime --color-2: orange;\n  }\n}\n\n.gradient-text {\n  animation: color-change 2s linear infinite alternate;\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n###  Make a few props, Swap em' in a dark MQ# \n\nTo keep things declarative, I've also defined color variables to hold the colors for animation.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_color-1-from: yellow;\n  --_color-1-to: orange;\n  --_color-2-from: purple;\n  --_color-2-to: hotpink;\n\n  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {\n    --_color-1-from: lime;\n    --_color-1-to: cyan;\n    --_color-2-from: cyan;\n    --_color-2-to: deeppink;\n  }\n\n  /* set our typed variables to the \"from\" values */\n  --color-1: var(--_color-1-from);\n  --color-2: var(--_color-2-from);\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nPut all those moments and reasons together, and we have arrived at the final snippet:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;css\n\n@property --color-1 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@property --color-2 {\n  syntax: \"\u003ccolor\u003e\";\n  inherits: false;\n  initial-value: #000;\n}\n\n@keyframes color-change {\n  to {\n    --color-1: var(--_color-1-to);\n    --color-2: var(--_color-2-to);\n  }\n}\n\n.gradient-text {\n  --_space: ;\n\n  /* light mode */\n  --_color-1-from: yellow;\n  --_color-1-to: orange;\n  --_color-2-from: purple;\n  --_color-2-to: hotpink;\n\n  /* dark mode */\n  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {\n    --_color-1-from: lime;\n    --_color-1-to: cyan;\n    --_color-2-from: cyan;\n    --_color-2-to: deeppink;\n  }\n\n  --color-1: var(--_color-1-from);\n  --color-2: var(--_color-2-from);\n\n  animation: color-change 2s linear infinite alternate;\n\n  background: linear-gradient(\n    to right var(--_space),\n    var(--color-1),\n    var(--color-2)\n  );\n\n  /* old browser support */\n  -webkit-background-clip: text;\n  -webkit-text-fill-color: transparent;\n\n  /* modern browser version */\n  background-clip: text;\n  color: transparent;\n\n  @supports (background: linear-gradient(in oklch, #fff, #fff)) {\n    --_space: in oklch;\n  }\n}\n\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n🤓 \n\nSome years these snippets are short and sweet, but not this year. Report Abuse \n\nCover image for Vintage photo effect with CSS \n\ndebadeepsen \n\ndebadeepsen \n\n Posted on Dec 22, 2020 • Edited on Aug 17, 2023 \n\n#  Vintage photo effect with CSS\n\n#css #html \n\nIf you, like me, were born in the eighties, you have probably spent some time going through old family photo albums. Back when an album was a physical object that you held in your hands. And even though cameras back in the day lacked the technological prowess of the modern day, the photos were still beautiful in their own way. As a hobbyist photographer myself, I have often used Photoshop and other tools to achieve vintage effects on photos that I took, and simpler tools like Instagram also exist to create similar looks. However, the front-end developer in me got thinking - is there a way to display a photo on the web, like it had been taken in the sixties or seventies? We're in luck, because as it turns out, there is.\n\n##  Display only\n\nOne thing that I should be clear about is that this is purely a display-based solution. Which means, the image file isn't manipulated in any way, nor can you save the altered image (other than by taking a screenshot).\n\n##  What we'll do\n\nTo make a photo appear \"vintage\", we will be doing the following:\n\n* Add a vignette, aka, a gradient-based darkening around the edges, which was often seen in photos taken by old cameras.\n* Give the picture a yellowish-orangeish tinge, to give the impression of aging.\n* Overlay a subtle film-grainy texture over the image.\n* Blur the image a little, because lenses in the past didn't always have tack-sharp focus.\n* Make some adjustments to brightness, contrast, and saturation.\n\nWe'll be using a few neat things that CSS3 allows us to do, so let's take a look at them now.\n\n##  Trick #1: Stacking background images.\n\nCSS3 lets you stack multiple background images, on top of one another. This can be used to create really nice-looking overlays (for example, you could make it look like the sun was peeking from behind the clouds, using different image assets for the sun and the clouds). To do so, we use the &#96;background-image&#96; property, and list the image sources separated by commas (the viewing order is start to finish, i.e., images will be placed over the ones succeeding them in the list).\n\nAnother neat thing about CSS is that it treats gradients as images as well. Which means, instead of just chaining multiple images together to form the &#96;background-image&#96; of an element, you could use a mix of gradients and images. We will use this fact to implement various parts of the filter.\n\n####  Vignette\n\nA vignette is literally a radial gradient. We'll use an elliptical shape for it. So the CSS for that would be somewhat like  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nbackground-image: radial-gradient(ellipse, #0000, #0007);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n####  Tint\n\nWe can use the &#96;linear-gradient&#96; function to add a translucent overlay. Note that, if we specify a gradient with two colors, and set the same values to both, it will behave as a solid block. While we don't need this technique normally, here we actually do, because remember - gradients are valid background images, regular solid colors are not.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nbackground-image: linear-gradient(0deg, #9725, #9725);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n\u003e A four digit hex code like &#96;#rgba&#96; is essentially a short way of writing &#96;#rrggbbaa&#96;, where &#96;aa&#96; denotes the alpha channel.\n\n####  Film grain\n\nTo obtain this effect, I generated a noise texture on \u003chttp://www.noisetexturegenerator.com/\u003e and added it as another layer of background image.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nbackground-image: url(https://i.ibb.co/vJt5HSh/noisy-texture-300x300-o10-d10-c-a82851-t1.png);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nFinally, combining everything and including the actual image to be displayed, we have the following background:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nbackground-image: radial-gradient(ellipse, #0000, #0007),\n            linear-gradient(0deg, #9725, #9725),\n            url(https://i.ibb.co/vJt5HSh/noisy-texture-300x300-o10-d10-c-a82851-t1.png),\n            url(https://i.ibb.co/m4sGRmK/pexels-pixabay-247431.jpg);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n##  Trick #2: CSS filters\n\nCSS filters work in the same way that most photo filters do these days - they add some cool visual effects. The best part is that with CSS, filters can be applied to any element, not just images, which opens up a host of possibilities. We'll use four filters here - &#96;blur&#96;, &#96;saturation&#96;, &#96;brightness&#96;, and &#96;contrast&#96;.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nfilter: blur(0.05rem) saturate(0.7) contrast(1.5) brightness(1.2);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n(Values here are only suggested values, play around with them as much as you want until you're satisfied with the result).\n\n##  Final CSS and result\n\nWith everything above (and a few other things) combined, here's how the final CSS class (I'm calling it &#96;filtered&#96;) would look like -  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n.filtered {\n    width: 800px;\n    height: 450px;\n    border-radius: 10px;\n    margin: 2px;\n    background-image: \n        radial-gradient(ellipse, #0000, #0007),\n        linear-gradient(0deg, #9725, #9725),\n        url(https://i.ibb.co/vJt5HSh/noisy-texture-300x300-o10-d10-c-a82851-t1.png),\n        url(https://i.ibb.co/m4sGRmK/pexels-pixabay-247431.jpg);\n    background-size: auto, auto, auto, cover;\n    background-repeat: repeat;\n    background-position: center;\n    filter: blur(0.05em) saturate(0.7) contrast(1.5) brightness(1.2);\n}\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n\u003e 1. Just like the &#96;background-image&#96;, the &#96;background-size&#96; and &#96;background-repeat&#96; properties can also be comma-chained. When we write it this way, each segment corresponds to each of the image sources specified as background source.\n\u003e 2. Unlike with the background, we don't use commas when chaining values for filter. Instead, they are separated by space.\n\nAnd that should do it. You can check out the sandbox I created below (with a little help from some friendly neighborhood JavaScript) that shows some beautiful photos (thanks to the wonderful \u003chttps://pexels.com\u003e) and their corresponding \"aged\" versions.\n\nOne last word, this method is just a suggestion - it's one way to achieve this effect. There are definitely other options. For example, instead of using the &#96;background-image&#96; property of a &#96;div&#96;, you could think of using the &#96;object-fit&#96; property of an &#96;img&#96; element directly. I also used two kinds of gradients here, but the same thing probably could have been done with a &#96;radial-gradient&#96;.\n\nHope you enjoyed the post. Until next time!\n\n##  Top comments (4) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCollapse Expand \n\nthomasbnt profile image \n\nThomas Bnt \n\n Thomas BntSubscriber \n\n Thomas Bnt \n\nFollow \n\n French web developer mainly but touches everything. Forced Color Adjust\n\n# Tailwind CSS Background Clip\n\nThe **&#96;background-clip&#96; CSS property** determines how the background image or color is applied to an element. By restricting its painting area, it can be confined to the element's border, padding, or content box, and even clipped to the visible parts of **text**. In Tailwind CSS, you gain **utilities** to use &#96;background-clip&#96; effectively, allowing you to style your layouts with precision and improved versatility. Let's explore how you can leverage these utilities in different scenarios.\n\n| Class           | Properties                    | Example                                 |\n| --------------- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |\n| bg-clip-border  | background-clip: border-box;  | \u003cdiv className=\"bg-clip-border\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e  |\n| bg-clip-padding | background-clip: padding-box; | \u003cdiv className=\"bg-clip-padding\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e |\n| bg-clip-content | background-clip: content-box; | \u003cdiv className=\"bg-clip-content\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e |\n| bg-clip-text    | background-clip: text;        | \u003cdiv className=\"bg-clip-text\"\u003e\u003c/div\u003e    |\n\n## Overview of Background Clip\n\n### Border\n\nTailwind CSS simplifies configuring &#96;background-clip&#96; by offering predefined **utility classes**. These classes enable you to apply clipping directly to elements without writing custom CSS. You can choose between distinct clipping behaviors such as &#96;border-box&#96;, &#96;padding-box&#96;, &#96;content-box&#96;, or even isolate background styles to text.\n\nThis is a live editor. Play around with it!\n\nexport default function App() {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"h-screen w-screen bg-gray-100 flex justify-center items-center\"\u003e\n      \u003cdiv\n        className=\"border-4 border-cyan-500 bg-clip-border bg-orange-300 border-dashed text-center p-6 rounded\"\n        /* Background is clipped to the border box */\n      \u003e\n        \u003ch1\u003eBackground Clip Border\u003c/h1\u003e\n      \u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n}\n\nThe output for &#96;bg-clip-border&#96; ensures that the **background property spans across the &#96;border-box&#96;.** Here, the orange background extends up to the element's border, emphasizing the visual effect of the borders.\n\n### Padding\n\nIf you aim to limit the background to stay **inside the padding**, Tailwind's &#96;bg-clip-padding&#96; is your utility. This ensures no portion of the background extends to the border.\n\nThis is a live editor. Play around with it!\n\nexport default function App() {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"h-screen w-screen bg-gray-100 flex justify-center items-center\"\u003e\n      \u003cdiv\n        className=\"border-4 border-red-400 border-dashed bg-clip-padding bg-teal-400 p-12 rounded shadow-lg\"\n        /* Background is clipped to the padding box */\n      \u003e\n        \u003ch1\u003eBackground Clip Padding\u003c/h1\u003e\n      \u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n}\n\nHere, only the **padding portion** gets the teal background, making the red border stand out distinctly.\n\n### Content\n\nTo paint the background solely within the **content area** of your element, consider &#96;bg-clip-content&#96;. This lets you exclude the padding and borders from receiving the style.\n\nThis is a live editor. Play around with it!\n\nexport default function App() {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"h-screen w-screen bg-gray-100 flex justify-center items-center\"\u003e\n      \u003cdiv\n        className=\"border-4 border-fuchsia-500 bg-clip-content bg-blue-500 px-12 py-8 text-gray-800 rounded\"\n        /* Background is restricted to the content box */\n      \u003e\n        \u003cp className=\"font-medium\"\u003e\n          Only the content visible for the background.\n        \u003c/p\u003e\n      \u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n}\n\nThis minimal rendering style ensures that the background remains **in the text's content block**, avoiding distraction from paddings or borders.\n\n### Text\n\nClipping to **text** is an excellent feature, especially for creating artistic and dynamic typography with images or gradients. By combining &#96;bg-clip-text&#96; with a transparent background color (**using &#96;text-transparent&#96; in Tailwind**), you can achieve attractive outcomes.\n\nThis is a live editor. Play around with it!\n\nexport default function App() {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"h-screen w-screen flex justify-center items-center bg-gray-800\"\u003e\n      \u003ch1\n        className=\"bg-clip-text text-transparent text-5xl font-extrabold bg-gradient-to-r from-green-400 via-blue-500 to-purple-500\"\n        /* Background is clipped to visible text */\n      \u003e\n        Vibrant Clipped Text\n      \u003c/h1\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n}\n\nHere, we used &#96;bg-gradient-to-r&#96; to create a gradient background clip, enriched with transitions between **green, blue, and violet hues.**\n\n## States and Responsiveness\n\n### Hover and Focus States\n\nTailwind allows you to conditionally apply styling on interactive states such as hover and focus. Here's an example:\n\nThis is a live editor. Play around with it!\n\nexport default function App() {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"h-screen w-screen flex justify-center items-center bg-gray-700\"\u003e\n      \u003cbutton\n        className=\"bg-clip-text text-transparent font-semibold text-4xl bg-blue-400 hover:bg-gradient-to-br hover:from-yellow-400 hover:to-red-500\"\n        /* Background changes on hover */\n      \u003e\n        Hover for Effect\n      \u003c/button\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n}\n\nTry hovering over the button to observe how the background transitions into a **blazing yellow-to-red gradient.** This approach makes your applications more engaging.\n\n### Breakpoint Modifiers\n\nCreating responsive layouts using **breakpoints** is an essential part of modern web development. Tailwind brings support for controlling &#96;background-clip&#96; per device screen size directly via utilities.\n\nThis is a live editor. Play around with it!\n\nexport default function App() {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"h-screen w-screen bg-gray-50 flex justify-center items-center\"\u003e\n      \u003cdiv\n        className=\"p-12 w-80 text-lg bg-orange-400 rounded-xl text-white text-center border-blue-700 border-dashed border-4 sm:bg-clip-border md:bg-clip-padding lg:bg-clip-content\"\n        /* Configure background clipping by screen */\n      \u003e\n        \u003cspan\u003eResize Window: Observe the Switch!\u003c/span\u003e\n      \u003c/div\u003e\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n}\n\nResize your browser window to witness the **background-clip behavior change** based on screen width thresholds. This dynamic customization ensures optimized UI for all devices.\n\n## Real World Examples\n\n### Product Features Grid with Gradient Text Effect\n\nThis example shows a features grid where each feature title has a gradient background clipped to text, creating an eye-catching effect.\n\nThis is a live editor. Play around with it!\n\nexport default function FeatureGrid() {\n  const features = [\n    {\n      title: \"Analytics Dashboard\",\n      description: \"Real-time data visualization and reporting\",\n      icon: \"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1551288049-bebda4e38f71?w=100\"\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Team Collaboration\",\n      description: \"Seamless team communication tools\",\n      icon: \"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1522071820081-009f0129c71c?w=100\"\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"API Integration\",\n      description: \"Connect with thousands of services\",\n      icon: \"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1558494949-ef010cbdcc31?w=100\"\n    },\n    {\n      title: \"Smart Automation\",\n      description: \"Automate repetitive tasks efficiently\",\n      icon: \"https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1518432031352-d6fc5c10da5a?w=100\"\n    },\n  ];\n\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"grid grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-3 gap-6 p-8\"\u003e\n      {features.map((feature, index) =\u003e (\n        \u003cdiv key={index} className=\"p-6 bg-white rounded-xl shadow-lg\"\u003e\n          \u003cimg \n            src={feature.icon} \n            alt={feature.title}\n            className=\"w-12 h-12 rounded-full mb-4\"\n          /\u003e\n          \u003ch3 className=\"text-3xl font-bold bg-gradient-to-r from-purple-600 to-pink-600 bg-clip-text text-transparent\"\u003e\n            {feature.title}\n          \u003c/h3\u003e\n          \u003cp className=\"mt-2 text-gray-600\"\u003e{feature.description}\u003c/p\u003e\n        \u003c/div\u003e\n      ))}\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n}\n\n### Testimonial Cards with Clipped Padding\n\nA testimonial section where each card has a background clipped to its padding box.\n\nThis is a live editor. Interfaces\n\nDesign consistency can be achieved by standardizing how &#96;background-clip&#96; is used for similar elements, such as buttons, headings, or banners. For instance, if your branding frequently uses &#96;bg-clip-text&#96; for gradients in headings, avoid deviating from that aesthetic for one-off instances. This approach helps users navigate content effortlessly while maintaining a harmonious and professional appearance across your UI.\n\nMoreover, when working on larger projects, integrate consistent &#96;background-clip&#96; patterns into design tokens or component libraries. This ensures future components continue to adhere to the original styling conventions while reducing the potential for design fragmentation. A common practice is to name reusable components semantically, such as &#96;StyledHeader&#96; or &#96;HighlightButton&#96;, that bundle tailored &#96;background-clip&#96; utilities with matching gradients or patterns.\n\nBy adhering to consistent &#96;background-clip&#96; usage, you minimize redundancy and styling errors. You should also actively review your components during code reviews, ensuring alignment with project design goals. Tools like Tailwind's &#96;@apply&#96; directive can help consolidate repetitive &#96;background-clip&#96; and other utilities, promoting reusability without unnecessary duplication.\n\n### Leverage Utility Combinations Thoughtfully\n\nIn Tailwind CSS, you can combine &#96;background-clip&#96; utilities with other classes such as gradients, padding modifiers, and typography utilities to craft visually appealing components. For instance, pairing &#96;bg-clip-text&#96; with &#96;bg-gradient-to-r&#96; and &#96;text-transparent&#96; is effective for creating gradient text highlights, perfect for branding headers or promotional content.\n\nWhen crafting components that involve complex designs, always combine utilities hierarchically. Start with structural styles like &#96;p-8&#96; or &#96;rounded-lg&#96;, then apply primary aesthetic utilities, e.g., &#96;bg-clip-padding&#96; with color properties like &#96;bg-green-400&#96;. Finally, add responsive utilities, e.g., &#96;md:bg-clip-border&#96; to allow breakpoint-specific customization. Combining utilities in a logical order helps avoid conflicts where one class inadvertently overrides another.\n\n## Accessibility Considerations\n\n### Enhance Readability and Navigation Clarity\n\nWhen designing interfaces with &#96;background-clip&#96;, always prioritize readability for users. For example, &#96;bg-clip-text&#96; may lead to blending issues when combined with low-contrast gradients or image overlays. To mitigate this, pair &#96;text-transparent&#96; with high-contrast gradients like &#96;bg-gradient-to-r from-blue-400 to-green-500&#96;, ensuring text remains legible against varying background patterns. Test your designs with contrast-checking tools to ensure they meet WCAG accessibility standards.\n\nClarity in navigation is equally critical. Avoid overly decorative &#96;background-clip&#96; applications on key navigational components such as menu items or actionable buttons, which could distract users. Instead, use it sparingly and reinforce user interactions with additional focus or hover states, e.g., &#96;hover:bg-clip-content focus:bg-clip-border&#96;. This facilitates enhanced navigability for both sighted and keyboard users, ensuring accessibility for a wider audience.\n\nAlways consider the experience of users leveraging screen magnification or smaller devices. // Use children for the label or content\n}\n\nexport const Button: React.FC\u003cButtonProps\u003e = ({\n  children,\n  variant = 'primary',\n  size = 'medium',\n  className = '',\n  ...props\n}) =\u003e {\n  const modeClass = styles[variant] || styles.primary;\n  const sizeClass = styles[size] || styles.medium;\n\n  return (\n    \u003cbutton\n      type=\"button\" // Default to type=\"button\" for accessibility unless overridden\n      className={&#96;${styles.buttonBase} ${modeClass} ${sizeClass} ${className}&#96;}\n      {...props}\n    \u003e\n      {children}\n    \u003c/button\u003e\n  );\n};\n &#96;&#96;\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.module.css&#96;** (Example using CSS Modules):\n\nCopy&#96;/* src/components/Button/Button.module.css */\n.buttonBase {\n  border: none;\n  padding: 10px 20px;\n  cursor: pointer;\n  font-family: inherit;\n  border-radius: 4px;\n  transition: background-color 0.2s ease-in-out, box-shadow 0.2s ease-in-out;\n  display: inline-flex;\n  align-items: center;\n  justify-content: center;\n  text-decoration: none; /* For anchor-like buttons */\n  font-weight: 700; /* Bolder for Montserrat */\n}\n\n.buttonBase:focus-visible {\n  outline: 2px solid var(--focus-ring-color, blue); /* Define --focus-ring-color in global styles */\n  outline-offset: 2px;\n}\n\n/* Variants */\n.primary {\n  background-color: var(--button-primary-bg, #007bff);\n  color: var(--button-primary-text, white);\n}\n.primary:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-primary-hover-bg, #0056b3);\n}\n\n.secondary {\n  background-color: var(--button-secondary-bg, #6c757d);\n  color: var(--button-secondary-text, white);\n}\n.secondary:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-secondary-hover-bg, #545b62);\n}\n\n.destructive {\n  background-color: var(--button-destructive-bg, #dc3545);\n  color: var(--button-destructive-text, white);\n}\n.destructive:hover {\n  background-color: var(--button-destructive-hover-bg, #c82333);\n}\n\n/* Sizes */\n.small {\n  padding: 6px 12px;\n  font-size: 0.875rem;\n}\n.medium {\n  padding: 10px 20px;\n  font-size: 1rem;\n}\n.large {\n  padding: 12px 24px;\n  font-size: 1.125rem;\n}\n&#96;\n\nEnsure you define CSS variables like &#96;--button-primary-bg&#96; // from Button.module.css, actual name might be mangled\n    // For specific variant/size classes, snapshot testing or visual testing is more robust.\n  });\n\n  test('calls onClick handler when clicked', () =\u003e {\n    const handleClick = jest.fn();\n    render(\u003cButton onClick={handleClick}\u003eTest Click\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Test Click'));\n    expect(handleClick).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);\n  });\n\n  test('is disabled when disabled prop is true', () =\u003e {\n    render(\u003cButton disabled\u003eDisabled Button\u003c/Button\u003e);\n    expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /Disabled Button/i })).toBeDisabled();\n  });\n});\n&#96;\n\n**Storybook for Development and Documentation:**\n\nInitialize Storybook in your project:\n\nCopy&#96;npx storybook@latest init&#96;\n\nFollow the prompts. It should detect your React setup.\n\n**&#96;src/components/Button/Button.stories.tsx&#96;**:\n\nCopy&#96;import React from 'react';\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Button, ButtonProps } from './Button';
