// Use ButtonProps for Story type\n\nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Primary Button',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Secondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'secondary',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Secondary Button',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Destructive: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'destructive',\n    size: 'medium',\n    children: 'Delete',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const LargePrimary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    size: 'large',\n    children: 'Large Primary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const SmallSecondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'secondary',\n    size: 'small',\n    children: 'Small Secondary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Disabled: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n    children: 'Disabled Button',\n    disabled: true,\n  },\n};\n&#96;\n\nRun Storybook with &#96;npm run storybook&#96;.\n\n## 6\\. Publishing \u0026 Versioning Your Library\n\nOnce your components are ready, you'll publish your library to a package registry (like npm or a private registry).\n\n**Update &#96;package.json&#96;** with necessary fields:\n\nCopy&#96;{\n  \"name\": \"my-react-ui-library\",\n  \"version\": \"0.1.0\",\n  \"private\": false, // Set to false to publish\n  \"description\": \"A fantastic React UI component library.\",\n  \"author\": \"Your Name \u003cyouremail@example.com\u003e\",\n  \"license\": \"MIT\", // Or your chosen license\n  \"repository\": {\n    \"type\": \"git\",\n    \"url\": \"https://github.com/yourusername/my-react-ui-library.git\" // Replace\n  },\n  \"main\": \"dist/index.cjs.js\", // CommonJS entry point from Rollup\n  \"module\": \"dist/index.esm.js\", // ES Module entry point from Rollup\n  \"types\": \"dist/types/index.d.ts\", // TypeScript definitions entry point\n  \"files\": [ // Files to include in the published package\n    \"dist\"\n  ],\n  \"scripts\": {\n    \"build\": \"rollup -c\", // Your build command\n    \"test\": \"jest\",\n    \"storybook\": \"storybook dev -p 6006\",\n    \"build-storybook\": \"storybook build\",\n    \"lint\": \"eslint src --ext .ts,.tsx\",\n    \"clean\": \"rm -rf dist\" // Script to clean the dist folder\n  },\n  \"peerDependencies\": { // Specify peer dependencies\n    \"react\": \"^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0\",\n    \"react-dom\": \"^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0\"\n  },\n  \"devDependencies\": {\n    // ... your dev dependencies ...\n  },\n  \"dependencies\": {\n    // \"tslib\": \"^2.x.x\" // tslib is often a runtime dependency when using --importHelpers in tsconfig or by some TS features\n  }\n}\n&#96;\n\n**Publishing Steps:**\n\n1. Ensure your code is committed and pushed to your Git repository.\n2. Build your library: &#96;npm run build&#96; (this should run Rollup and tsc for declarations).\n3. Log in to npm (or your private registry): &#96;npm login&#96;.\n4. Update the version (semantic versioning is recommended):&#96;npm version patch&#96; (for bug fixes: 0.1.0 -\u003e 0.1.1)  \n&#96;npm version minor&#96; (for new features, non-breaking: 0.1.0 -\u003e 0.2.0)  \n&#96;npm version major&#96; (for breaking changes: 0.1.0 -\u003e 1.0.0)\n5. Publish: &#96;npm publish&#96; (add &#96;--access public&#96; if publishing a scoped package to npm for the first time).\n6. Push tags to Git: &#96;git push --tags&#96;.\n\nConsider using tools like &#96;semantic-release&#96; to automate the versioning and publishing process based on commit messages.\n\n## 7\\. Advanced Considerations for Robust Libraries\n\nAs your library grows, consider these advanced topics:\n\n* **Accessibility (A11y):**  \n   * Go beyond basic ARIA attributes. Ensure full keyboard navigability for all interactive components.  \n   * Test with screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS).  \n   * Manage focus states meticulously, especially for modals, dropdowns, and other overlay components.  \n   * Use tools like &#96;@axe-core/react&#96; for automated accessibility checks during development and testing.  \n   * Provide clear documentation on any accessibility implications of your components.\n* **Theming Strategies:**  \n   * **CSS Custom Properties (Variables):** Highly recommended for modern libraries. Define a set of global and component-specific CSS variables for colors, fonts, spacing, etc. Consumers can then override these variables to theme the library.  \n   * **React Context API:** For more dynamic theming or when CSS variables are insufficient (e.g., switching between light/dark mode which might involve more than just CSS). Provide a ThemeProvider component.  \n   * **Styled-components / Emotion Theming:** If using CSS-in-JS, leverage their built-in theming capabilities.  \n   * Document clearly how to apply and customize themes.\n* **Performance Optimization:**  \n   * Use &#96;React.memo&#96; for functional components and &#96;shouldComponentUpdate&#96; (or &#96;PureComponent&#96;) for class components to prevent unnecessary re-renders.  \n   * Memoize expensive calculations with &#96;useMemo&#96; and callbacks with &#96;useCallback&#96;.  \n   * Be mindful of bundle size. Analyze your bundle with tools like &#96;rollup-plugin-visualizer&#96; or &#96;webpack-bundle-analyzer&#96;.  \n   * Lazy load components or parts of your library if they are not immediately needed.  \n   * Ensure efficient event handling and avoid memory leaks.\n* **Developing Utility Hooks \u0026 Data Connectors (Helpers):**  \n   * For internal tools, you might identify common data fetching patterns or interactions with specific internal APIs/databases.  \n   * Create custom hooks (e.g., &#96;useInternalApi(endpoint, options)&#96;) that encapsulate this logic. These hooks are part of your library but are not UI components.  \n   * These hooks can handle loading states, error handling, and data transformation, making it easier for consuming applications to interact with backends consistently.  \n   Copy&#96;&#96; // Example: src/hooks/useQueryData.ts  \n   import { useState, useEffect, useCallback } from 'react';  \n   interface QueryDataOptions {  \n     // Define options: method, headers, body etc.  \n     method?: 'GET' | 'POST' | 'PUT' | 'DELETE';  \n     headers?: Record\u003cstring, string\u003e;  \n     body?: any;  \n   }  \n   export function useQueryData\u003cT\u003e(url: string, options?: QueryDataOptions) {  \n     const [data, setData] = useState\u003cT | null\u003e(null);  \n     const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);  \n     const [error, setError] = useState\u003cError | null\u003e(null);  \n     const fetchData = useCallback(async () =\u003e {  \n       setLoading(true);  \n       setError(null);  \n       try {  \n         const fetchOptions = {  \n           method: options?.method || 'GET',  \n           headers: {  \n             'Content-Type': 'application/json',  \n             ...options?.headers,  \n           },  \n           body: options?.body ? JSON.stringify(options.body) : undefined,  \n         };  \n         // Replace with your actual fetch logic, error handling, auth etc.  \n         const response = await fetch(url, fetchOptions);  \n         if (!response.ok) {  \n           throw new Error(&#96;HTTP error! status: ${response.status}&#96;);  \n         }  \n         const result = await response.json();  \n         setData(result);  \n       } catch (e) {  \n         setError(e as Error);  \n       } finally {  \n         setLoading(false);  \n       }  \n     }, [url, options]); // Consider options dependency carefully if it's not stable  \n     useEffect(() =\u003e {  \n       fetchData();  \n     }, [fetchData]); // Re-run if fetchData changes (due to url/options change)  \n     return { data, loading, error, refetch: fetchData };  \n   }  \n    &#96;&#96;\n* **Contribution Guidelines \u0026 Code Review:**  \n   * If multiple engineers contribute, establish clear guidelines: coding style (use Prettier and ESLint), commit message conventions, branching strategy (e.g., Gitflow), and PR process.  \n   * Enforce code reviews to maintain quality, share knowledge, and ensure consistency.  \n   * Automate checks with linters and formatters in your CI pipeline.\n* **Internationalization (i18n) and Localization (l10n):**  \n   * If your internal tools need to support multiple languages, plan for i18n from the start. This might involve passing locale props or using a context-based i18n library.\n* **Visual Regression Testing:**  \n   * Tools like Chromatic (by Storybook maintainers), Percy, or Applitools can help catch unintended visual changes in your components.\n\n## 8\\. Conclusion \u0026 Best Practices\n\nBuilding a high-quality **React component library** is an iterative process that requires careful planning, robust tooling, and a commitment to best practices. As an engineer, your focus should be on:\n\n* **Component Design:** Create flexible, composable, and accessible components with clear APIs.\n* **Code Quality:** Write clean, maintainable, and well-typed TypeScript code.\n* **Thorough Testing:** Implement comprehensive unit, integration, and potentially visual regression tests.\n* **Excellent Documentation:** Use Storybook effectively to provide interactive examples and clear usage guidelines. Engineers are key contributors to good documentation.\n* **Collaboration:** If working in a team, follow established contribution guidelines and participate actively in code reviews.\n* **Continuous Improvement:** Regularly revisit and refactor components, optimize for performance, and incorporate feedback from users of the library.\n\nA well-crafted component library will significantly improve the efficiency, consistency, and quality of your organization's internal tools, making it a valuable asset for the engineering team.\n\nDinesh Kumar, VP Engineering, Yubi Group \n\n### \"We didnt build our library for internal tools; we rather used DronaHQ low code platform!\"\n\n \"Building and maintaining our own React component library was a huge time sink. We switched to **DronaHQ**, a visual dev tool, and it's made building internal tools **10x simpler and faster** for our entire engineering team. Now we focus on solving business problems, not UI plumbing.\"\n\n Dinesh Kumar\n\n VP Engineering, Yubi Group\n\n Simplify Your Internal Tooling → ",

Storybook best practices for making the most out of Nx\n\n# Storybook best practices for making the most out of Nx\n\n## Purpose of this guide\n\nThe purpose of this guide is to help you set up Storybook in your Nx workspace so that you can get the most out of Nx and its powerful capabilities.\n\n## When to use Storybook\n\nUsually, Storybook is mainly used for two reasons. Testing and documentation. You can read more on when and why to use Storybook in the Why Storybook in 2022? article and also in the Introduction to Storybook documentation page.\n\n### Testing\n\nStorybook helps you test your UIs. You can read more about testing with Storybook in the How to test your UIs with Storybook documentation page. Essentially, Storybook uses the stories as a starting point for testing.\n\n### Documentation\n\nStorybook helps you document your UI elements, or your design system, effectively and in an interactive way. You can read more in the How to document components documentation page. Essentially, you can use Storybook to publish a catalog of your components. A catalog that you can share with the design team, the developer team, the product team, anyone else in the product development process, or even the client. The components are isolated, interactive, and can be represented in all possible forms that they can take (e.g. for a button: enabled, disabled, active, etc). You can read more about publishing your Storybook in the Publish Storybook documentation page.\n\n## Nx and Storybook\n\nNow let’s see how Nx can be used to accommodate both of these pillars of Storybook. Nx takes lots of the burden off your arms when setting up Storybook initially. It essentially provides you with all that you need to start using Storybook’s capabilities (testing and documentation) right away, without having to write a single line of code.\n\n### Development tools\n\nFirst, let’s see what Nx offers, when you are in the process of developing a project with Storybook.\n\n#### Configuration generation\n\nYou can generate the Storybook configuration files and settings using the Nx @nx/storybook:configuration generator. You can read more about configuring Storybook with Nx in our @nx/storybook introduction page. With Nx, you configure Storybook for each individual project.\n\n#### Stories generation\n\nIf you are on a project using Angular, React or React Native, you can also generate stories for your components. You can do so either by using each package's &#96;storybook-configuration&#96; generators or by using the &#96;stories&#96; generator, if you already have Storybook configured for your project.\n\nIf your project is not configured yet, check out one of these guides:\n\n* Set up Storybook for React (and Next.js) Projects\n* Set up Storybook for Angular Projects\n* Set up Storybook for Vue Projects\n\nIf your project is already configured, you can use the &#96;stories&#96; generator:\n\n* React (and Next.js) stories generator\n* Angular stories generator\n* Vue stories generator\n\nThe stories generator will read your inputs (if you’re using Angular), or your props (if you're using React), and will generate stories with the corresponding arguments/controls already prefilled.\n\n#### Storybook interaction tests\n\nStorybook interaction tests allow you to test user interactions within your Storybook stories. It enhances your Storybook setup, ensuring that not only do your components look right, but they also work correctly when interacted with.\n\nNx will generate interaction tests for your stories. You can read more in our Setting up Storybook Interaction Tests with Nx guide.\n\n### CI/CD tools\n\nNow let’s see how Nx helps in the CI/CD journey, as well.\n\n#### Interaction tests in your CI\n\nYou can set up your interaction tests to run as part of your CI. You can read more in the Storybook docs.\n\n#### Serve\n\nWhen you are configuring Storybook, Nx adds a serve and a build target for Storybook in your &#96;project.json&#96;, as we explained above. You can use these targets to serve and build storybook locally, and also in production. Cypress will also use these targets when firing up the e2e tests. While developing, you can serve your Storybooks locally to see if your components work and look as expected. This can help you and speed up the development and debugging process (no need to fire up a complex dev stack).\n\n#### Build and deploy\n\nThe build and deploy step usually comes in handy when you are ready to use Storybook for documentation, and you want to publish it. The building step of Storybook is integrated in the Nx ecosystem, as explained above, and you can trigger your Storybook builds as you would trigger any other build inside your workspace.\n\nWhen you publish your organization’s Storybook, as a result, ideally, you would want to have one shareable Storybook page/application living under one URL, that you can share. With Nx, you can build your Storybook and it will be ready for deployment. **However**, at this point, you have one Storybook per project in your workspace, and you could end up with far too many Storybooks that are built and ready for deployment. This is not ideal, and does not accomplish the ultimate goal of “one shareable documentation page”.\n\nIn the following section, we are going to see how to set up Storybook in these cases, to get the most out of Nx.\n\n## How to set up Storybook to get the most out of Nx\n\n### Philosophy\n\nSetting up Storybook on Nx reflects - and takes advantage of - the mental model of Nx. What that means, in essence, is that you still maintain the individual Storybook instances (per project) which you use for testing and local development, but you also keep one extra “container” for publishing, that serves as a single entry point. Let’s see this in more detail.\n\n#### Local development and testing\n\n##### Development and debugging\n\nIn the process of setting up Storybook in your Nx workspace that we described above, you end up with one Storybook instance per project. That way, you can use your project’s Storybook targets to serve, test and build Storybook:\n\n❯\n\nnx storybook my-project\n\nand\n\n❯\n\nnx build-storybook my-project\n\nand\n\n❯\n\nnx test-storybook my-project\n\nThis feature is extremely useful when developing locally. The containerized stories in your Storybook are the only ones that are built/served/tested when you want to debug just one component, or just one library. You don’t have to wait for a huge Storybook containing all your stories in your repository to fire up. You just need to wait for the Storybook of a single project to start. This speeds up the process.\n\n##### Caching, affected, dependency management\n\nSince each Storybook, in this case, is attached to a project, so is the serving of Storybook and the building of Storybook and the e2e tests for that project. That means that Nx is aware of these tasks, so it caches them, it knows when to fetch them from the cache or re-run them according to the affected status of that project. It also knows that project’s dependencies and knows which things to rebuild before each task.\n\n#### Publishing\n\nWhen you are publishing your Storybook, you can follow the principles described in the project size decision page. The general idea is to have one central Storybook container, into which you are going to gather your stories from multiple libraries.\n\nYou can think of the central Storybook container as a grouping of similar-concept or same-scope UI parts of your workspace. In the same way you are scoping libraries, you can group your stories as well.\n\nThen, according to your use-case, you can have one central Storybook for your whole workspace, importing all the stories from all the projects. Alternatively, you can have one Storybook per \"scope\", which imports all the stories from projects the same scope. Or even one Storybook per application, importing all the stories of all the libraries that it is depending on. As you can see, there are many options, and you can choose the one that best suits your needs.\n\nStorybook Composition\n\nIn order to achieve some things mentioned above, you may use Storybook Composition. However, in this case, you would still need to build each project’s Storybook individually, and also deploy it individually. So in the cases where you have multiple projects, Storybook Composition would not be very efficient.\n\nBefore moving on to the examples section, it could be useful to read the Library Types documentation page and the Grouping libraries documentation page. These could help you decide which way fits your use case better.\n\n## Examples / Use cases\n\nYou can check out the following examples (recipes) to see publishing strategies for Storybook in Nx:\n\n* One main Storybook instance for all projects\n* One Storybook instance per scope\n* One main Storybook instance using Storybook Composition\n\n## Conclusion\n\nIn this guide, we have given a direction towards the most efficient way to use Storybook in a Nx workspace, in a way that takes advantage of the all that Nx has to offer. We have covered the different ways to set up Storybook, and publish it, too. We have also covered the different use cases that apply to each of the solutions.\n\nIf you have any questions or suggestions, please feel free to reach out to us on GitHub, and don't hesitate to ask your questions or share your stories in the Official Nx Discord Server.\n\n### Nx \u0026 Storybook documentation\n\nYou can find all Storybook-related Nx documentation in the packages page.\n\n26.5k\n\nGive us a Star!\n\nOn this page\n* Overview\n* Purpose of this guide\n* When to use Storybook\n* Testing\n* Documentation\n* Nx and Storybook\n* Development tools\n* CI/CD tools\n* How to set up Storybook to get the most out of Nx\n* Philosophy\n* Examples / Use cases\n* Conclusion\n* Nx \u0026 Storybook documentation\n\nFeedback\n\nEdit this page\n\nFeedbackEdit this page\n\n## Footer\n\nNx\n\nSmart Repos · Fast Builds\n\nDiscordGitHubXBlueskyYoutubeLinkedInNewsletter\n\nStatusSecurity\n\nTheme \n\nTheme\n\n### Resources\n\n* Blog\n* Youtube\n* Community\n* Customers\n\n### Solutions\n\n* Nx\n* Nx Cloud\n* Nx Enterprise\n\n### Nx Cloud\n\n* App\n* Docs\n* Pricing\n* Terms\n\n### Company\n\n* About us\n* Careers\n* Brands \u0026 Guidelines\n* Contact us\n\n© 2025 made with  by ",

Report Abuse \n\nCover image for A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation \n\nAustin Welsh \n\nAustin Welsh \n\n Posted on Feb 17 \n\n#  A Guide to Storybook: UI Development, Testing, and Documentation\n\n#webdev #ui #react #javascript \n\n👋 **Let's Connect!** Follow me on GitHub for new projects.\n\n---\n\n## **Introduction** \n\nBuilding **consistent and scalable UI components** is crucial in modern web development. **Storybook** is a tool that allows developers to **isolate, develop, test, and document UI components** in a sandboxed environment. \n\nStorybook enables you to:  \n  \n✅ **Develop components in isolation** without running a full application.  \n  \n✅ **Create a component library** for design consistency.  \n  \n✅ **Test and document UI behavior** interactively.  \n  \n✅ **Integrate with frameworks like React, Vue, Angular, and more**. \n\nIn this comprehensive guide, we’ll cover: \n\n* **Setting up Storybook**\n* **Writing and organizing stories**\n* **Using add-ons and controls**\n* **Testing components with Storybook**\n* **Mocking API requests**\n* **Visual regression testing**\n* **Automating accessibility testing**\n* **Snapshot testing**\n* **Theming in Storybook**\n* **Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E testing**\n* **Deploying Storybook as documentation**\n* **Best practices for Storybook projects**\n\n---\n\n##  What is Storybook?\n\nStorybook is an open-source tool for **building UI components in isolation**. It provides a dedicated environment for testing and documenting components **without running the entire application**. \n\n### **Why Use Storybook?** \n\n| Feature                                                | Storybook |\n| ------------------------------------------------------ | --------- |\n| Develop components **in isolation**                    | ✅ Yes     |\n| Interactive **component preview**                      | ✅ Yes     |\n| Built-in **documentation generation**                  | ✅ Yes     |\n| Supports **multiple frameworks** (React, Vue, Angular) | ✅ Yes     |\n| Integration with **Jest, Testing Library, Playwright** | ✅ Yes     |\n\n---\n\n##  Installing and Setting Up Storybook\n\nStorybook can be installed in a new or existing project. \n\n### **Installation for React** \n\nRun the following command in your project directory:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook@latest init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Automatically detects the framework and **configures Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ Generates a &#96;.storybook&#96; folder with configuration files.  \n  \n✔ Creates example stories to get started. \n\n### **Starting Storybook** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStorybook will launch on &#96;http://localhost:6006/&#96;.\n\n---\n\n##  Writing Your First Story\n\nA **story** represents a UI component's **state**. It defines how the component should appear in different scenarios. \n\n### **Basic Button Story (React Example)** \n\nCreate a file **&#96;Button.stories.js&#96;** inside &#96;src/components/Button/&#96;.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport React from 'react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\nexport default {\n  title: 'Components/Button',\n  component: Button,\n};\n\nexport const Primary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Primary Button\" /\u003e;\nexport const Secondary = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Secondary Button\" variant=\"secondary\" /\u003e;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each **export** represents a different **state of the component**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;title&#96; defines the **category in Storybook**.  \n  \n✔ &#96;component&#96; links the **UI component** to the story. \n\n---\n\n##  Using Controls for Dynamic Interaction\n\nStorybook Controls allow developers to modify props dynamically in the UI.\n\n###  Example: Adding Controls to Button\n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nexport const Playground = (args) =\u003e \u003cButton {...args} /\u003e;\n\nPlayground.args = {\n  label: 'Dynamic Button',\n  variant: 'primary',\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nNow, Storybook will provide a UI panel where developers can change **label** and **variant** dynamically.\n\n✔ Helps **test different states** without modifying the code.\n\n---\n\n##  Enhancing Storybook with Add-ons\n\nStorybook Add-ons extend functionality.\n\n###  Popular Storybook Add-ons\n\n| Add-on                     | Purpose                  |\n| -------------------------- | ------------------------ |\n| @storybook/addon-controls  | Adjust props dynamically |\n| @storybook/addon-docs      | Generate documentation   |\n| @storybook/addon-a11y      | Accessibility testing    |\n| @storybook/testing-library | UI interaction testing   |\n\n###  Installing an Add-on\n\nExample: Installing the **Accessibility Add-on**  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @storybook/addon-a11y --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; to **register the add-on**:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Adds an \"Accessibility\" panel to test contrast, ARIA attributes, and color issues.\n\n---\n\n##  Organizing Stories for Scalability\n\nA well-structured Storybook project improves maintainability. \n\n### **Recommended Folder Structure** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n📂 src\n ┣ 📂 components\n ┃ ┣ 📂 Button\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.stories.js\n ┃ ┃ ┣ 📜 Button.test.js\n ┣ 📂 .storybook\n ┃ ┣ 📜 main.js   # Configurations\n ┃ ┣ 📜 preview.js  # Global decorators\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Each component has **its own folder** for easy organization.  \n  \n✔ &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96; manages **configurations** and **add-ons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Automating Accessibility Testing in Storybook\n\nEnsuring your UI components are **accessible** is crucial for usability. Storybook integrates with **accessibility testing tools** to automatically detect potential issues.\n\n### **Installing the Accessibility Add-on** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-a11y\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Enabling the Add-on** \n\nModify &#96;.storybook/main.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nmodule.exports = {\n  addons: ['@storybook/addon-a11y'],\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Accessibility Tests** \n\nWhen the Storybook UI loads, a new **\"Accessibility\" panel** appears, displaying any detected issues.\n\n✔ Automatically **checks for contrast issues, missing ARIA attributes, and keyboard accessibility**.  \n  \n✔ Helps fix **WCAG compliance issues** before production. \n\n---\n\n##  Visual Regression Testing in Storybook\n\n**Visual Regression Testing** detects UI changes by comparing rendered components **before and after updates**. This ensures that UI modifications do not introduce **unintended design changes**.\n\n### **Installing Visual Testing Add-ons** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @storybook/addon-visual-tests\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Adding a Screenshot Test** \n\nModify &#96;Button.stories.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { within, userEvent } from '@storybook/testing-library';\n\nexport const VisualTest = () =\u003e \u003cButton label=\"Click me\" /\u003e;\n\nVisualTest.play = async ({ canvasElement }) =\u003e {\n  const canvas = within(canvasElement);\n  const button = canvas.getByRole('button');\n  await userEvent.click(button);\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running Visual Tests** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Detects UI changes with **automatic snapshot comparisons**. \n\n---\n\n##  Mocking API Calls in Storybook\n\nStorybook can mock API requests to test UI behavior without relying on a backend.\n\n###  Example: Mocking an API Response\n\nInstall Mock Service Worker (MSW):  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install msw --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;mocks.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { setupWorker, rest } from 'msw';\n\nexport const worker = setupWorker(\n  rest.get('/api/user', (req, res, ctx) =\u003e {\n    return res(ctx.json({ name: 'Mock User' }));\n  })\n);\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nStart the mock server in &#96;preview.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { worker } from '../mocks';\n\nworker.start();\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Components now receive mock API responses during development.\n\n---\n\n##  Integrating Storybook with Playwright for E2E Testing\n\nStorybook can be used with **Playwright** to perform **end-to-end (E2E) testing** for UI components.\n\n### **Installing Playwright** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install --save-dev @playwright/test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Writing a Playwright Test for a Storybook Component** \n\nCreate a file &#96;Button.spec.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nconst { test, expect } = require('@playwright/test');\n\ntest('Check if Button component renders', async ({ page }) =\u003e {\n    await page.goto('http://localhost:6006/?path=/story/components-button--primary');\n    const button = await page.locator('button');\n    await expect(button).toHaveText('Primary Button');\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n### **Running the Playwright Test** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx playwright test\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ **Combines UI component testing with full browser automation**. \n\n---\n\n##  Writing Component Tests in Storybook\n\nStorybook integrates with Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright for UI testing.\n\n###  Example: Testing with Jest + Testing Library\n\nInstall dependencies:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install @testing-library/react jest --save-dev\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nCreate &#96;Button.test.js&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nimport { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';\nimport Button from './Button';\n\ntest('renders the button', () =\u003e {\n  render(\u003cButton label=\"Click Me\" /\u003e);\n  expect(screen.getByText('Click Me')).toBeInTheDocument();\n});\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Ensures components render correctly.  \n✔ Runs with npm test.\n\n---\n\n##  Deploying Storybook as Documentation\n\nStorybook can be deployed as a **component documentation site**.\n\n### **Generate Static Build** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run build-storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis creates a **&#96;storybook-static/&#96;** folder.\n\n### **Deploy to GitHub Pages** \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Makes Storybook accessible via **GitHub Pages or any static host**. \n\n---\n\n##  Running Storybook in CI/CD\n\nIntegrating Storybook in CI/CD pipelines ensures UI consistency across development.\n\n###  GitHub Actions Example\n\nCreate &#96;.github/workflows/storybook.yml&#96;:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nname: Storybook CI\non: push\njobs:\n  test:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - name: Checkout Code\n        uses: actions/checkout@v2\n      - name: Install Dependencies\n        run: npm install\n      - name: Build Storybook\n        run: npm run build-storybook\n      - name: Deploy Storybook\n        run: npx storybook-to-ghpages\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n✔ Runs Storybook on every code push.\n\n---\n\n##  Best Practices for Storybook Projects\n\n✔ **Use Controls \u0026 Docs Add-ons** for **dynamic component interaction**.  \n  \n✔ **Organize components by category** (&#96;Components/Button&#96; vs &#96;Components/Inputs&#96;).  \n  \n✔ **Automate visual \u0026 snapshot testing** to **catch unintended changes**.  \n  \n✔ **Deploy Storybook** as **live documentation** for developers \u0026 designers.  \n  \n✔ **Integrate Storybook in CI/CD** to ensure UI consistency. \n\n---\n\n## **Conclusion** \n\nStorybook is a **powerful tool for UI development, testing, and documentation**. It improves **component reusability, consistency, and collaboration** across teams. \n\n🚀 **Next Steps:**  \n  \n✅ Install Storybook and create your first component story.  \n  \n✅ Experiment with **Controls \u0026 Add-ons**.  \n  \n✅ Integrate Storybook into your **CI/CD pipeline**. \n\n---\n\n### **Tags** \n\nStorybook #Frontend #Testing #UIDevelopment #ComponentLibrary \n\n---\n\n###  TLDR – Highlights for Skimmers\n\n* Storybook isolates UI components for development and testing.\n* Controls allow dynamic prop changes inside Storybook UI.\n* Add-ons extend functionality (accessibility, documentation, testing).\n* Supports Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright for UI testing.\n* Mocks API responses with MSW for frontend testing.\n* Can be deployed as documentation on GitHub Pages or other platforms.\n\n---\n\n💬 **Have you used Storybook?** Share your experience in the comments!\n\n##  Top comments (1) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCollapse Expand \n\naustinwdigital profile image \n\nAustin Welsh \n\n Austin Welsh \n\n Austin Welsh \n\nFollow \n\n Senior Full Stack Developer @ Disney | JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Next.js\n\n* Location  \n United States\n* Work  \n Senior Full Stack Developer @ Disney\n* Joined  \nDec 21, 2024\n\n•  Feb 17 \n\nDropdown menu \n\n* Copy link\n* Hide\n\nWhat do you mainly use Storybook for?\n\nA) Component Development  \nB) UI Testing  \nC) Documentation  \nD) Something else\n\nLet me know!\n\nLike comment: Like comment: 1 like  Like Comment button Reply \n\n Some comments may only be visible to logged-in visitors. They maintain state and run continuously, routing events to workflows and functions.\n\nLearn about Agents \n\n### Code in Python or TypeScript\n\nWrite code using simple libraries in Python or TypeScript.\n\nRestack libraries \n\nRestack\n\npythontypescript\n\nfrom restack_ai.workflow import workflow\n\n\n@workflow.defn()\n\nclass Workflow:\n\n    @workflow.run\n\n    async def run(self):\n\n\n        welcome_message = await workflow.step(welcome)\n\n\n        goodbye_message = await workflow.step(goodbye)\n\n\n        return goodbye_message\n\n### Long-running background workflows\n\nRun tasks that keep working for days, months, or years. Report Abuse \n\nCover image for Building and Documenting UI Components with Storybook and React \n\nDebajit Mallick \n\nDebajit Mallick \n\n Posted on Mar 23 \n\n#  Building and Documenting UI Components with Storybook and React\n\n#react #storybook #frontend #documentation \n\n##  Introduction\n\nHave you ever struggled with maintaining consistency across your UI components or found it challenging to collaborate with designers? I've been there too. After experimenting with several tools, I discovered that Storybook changed my development workflow for the better.\n\nIn this post, I'll walk you through setting up Storybook in a React project and show you how to build and document components that you can reuse throughout your applications.\n\n##  What is Storybook?\n\nIt lets you build and test UI components in isolation, away from the complexity of the full app. The interactive documentation makes it easier for team members to understand how components work. Using Storybook, Setting up visual regression tests became surprisingly simple\n\n##  Getting Started: Project Setup\n\nLet's start by creating our project foundation. Fire up your terminal and run:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm create vite@latest my-storybook-app -- --template react-ts\ncd my-storybook-app\nnpm install\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nWith our React project ready, let's add Storybook to the mix:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpx storybook@latest init\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis command works like magic – it automatically configures Storybook for your Vite setup, creates a &#96;.storybook/&#96; folder, and adds some example stories in &#96;src/stories/&#96;. Take a moment to explore these files to get familiar with the structure.\n\n##  Creating Our First Component: The Button\n\nLet's start by building a flexible Button component that we can reuse across our application.\n\nFirst, create the component file:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Button.tsx\nimport React from 'react';\n\nexport interface ButtonProps {\n  label: string;\n  onClick?: () =\u003e void;\n  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary';\n}\n\nexport const Button: React.FC\u003cButtonProps\u003e = ({\n  label,\n  onClick,\n  variant = 'primary',\n}) =\u003e {\n  const styles = {\n    primary: 'bg-blue-500 text-white',\n    secondary: 'bg-gray-200 text-black',\n  };\n\n  return (\n    \u003cbutton\n      className={&#96;px-4 py-2 rounded ${styles[variant]}&#96;}\n      onClick={onClick}\n    \u003e\n      {label}\n    \u003c/button\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nNow for the fun part – creating stories for our Button:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Button.stories.tsx\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Button\u003e = {\n  title: 'Components/Button',\n  component: Button,\n};\n\nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Button\u003e;\n\nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    label: 'Click Me',\n    variant: 'primary',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const Secondary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    label: 'Cancel',\n    variant: 'secondary',\n  },\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\n##  Building a Card Component\n\nNow that we have our Button, let's create a Card component that can even incorporate our Button.  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Card.tsx\nimport React from 'react';\n\nexport interface CardProps {\n  title: string;\n  description: string;\n  children?: React.ReactNode;\n}\n\nexport const Card: React.FC\u003cCardProps\u003e = ({ title, description, children }) =\u003e {\n  return (\n    \u003cdiv className=\"border rounded-lg shadow-md p-4 max-w-sm\"\u003e\n      \u003ch3 className=\"text-lg font-bold mb-2\"\u003e{title}\u003c/h3\u003e\n      \u003cp className=\"text-gray-700 mb-4\"\u003e{description}\u003c/p\u003e\n      {children}\n    \u003c/div\u003e\n  );\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nAnd here's how we can showcase it in Storybook:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// src/components/Card.stories.tsx\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/react';\nimport { Card } from './Card';\nimport { Button } from './Button';\n\nconst meta: Meta\u003ctypeof Card\u003e = {\n  title: 'Components/Card',\n  component: Card,\n};\n\nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof Card\u003e;\n\nexport const Default: Story = {\n  args: {\n    title: 'Welcome!',\n    description: 'This is a sample card component.',\n  },\n};\n\nexport const WithButton: Story = {\n  render: (args) =\u003e (\n    \u003cCard {...args}\u003e\n      \u003cButton label=\"Learn More\" /\u003e\n    \u003c/Card\u003e\n  ),\n  args: {\n    title: 'Interactive Card',\n    description: 'This card includes a button as a child component.',\n  },\n};\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nI particularly love this example because it shows how components can be nested in Storybook stories, helping you visualize complex component relationships.\n\n##  Adding Some Style with Tailwind (Optional)\n\nIf you're like me and prefer Tailwind for styling, it's super easy to add:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm install -D tailwindcss postcss autoprefixer\nnpx tailwindcss init -p\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nUpdate your CSS with:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n/* in index.css */\n@tailwind base;\n@tailwind components;\n@tailwind utilities;\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nDon't forget to add your source folder to the content paths in &#96;tailwind.config.js&#96;!\n\n##  Time to See It in Action!\n\nLet's fire up Storybook and see our components:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nWhen you visit \u003chttp://localhost:6006/\u003e, you'll see your Button and Card components displayed in the Storybook UI. Try clicking around and interacting with different props – it's incredibly satisfying to see your components respond in real-time.\n\n##  Sharing Your Component Library\n\nWant to share your beautiful components with the team or showcase them in a portfolio? Generate a static build:  \n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nnpm run build-storybook\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nEnter fullscreen mode Exit fullscreen mode \n\nThis creates a &#96;storybook-static/&#96; directory that you can deploy to Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages, or any static hosting provider. I've found this especially useful when working with remote teams.\n\n##  Conclusion\n\nUsing Storybook you can develop a consistent design system. Which helps you to onboard new team members more quickly, catch UI bugs before they reach production. Also, you can Communicate more effectively with designers. If you like this blog and want to learn more about **Frontend Development** and **Software Engineering**, you can follow me on Dev.to.\n\n##  Top comments (0) \n\nSubscribe \n\npic \n\nPersonal Trusted User \n\n Create template \n\nTemplates let you quickly answer FAQs or store snippets for re-use.\n\nSubmit Preview Dismiss \n\nCode of Conduct • Report abuse \n\n Are you sure you want to hide this comment?       "chunk": "DocsAddonsShowcaseBlogVisual TestEnterprise\n\n87,366\n\nSearch docs\n\n⌃K\n\nBack to blog\n\nJoin the community:\n\n# Storybook 9\n\nThe lean, mean component testing machine\n\nloading\n\nMichael Shilman\n\nJun 03, 2025 — @mshilman\n\nLast updated: Jun 03, 2025\n\nStorybook’s superpower is showing every possible state of your UI in one place, from a basic button to an obscure page. That makes it the perfect foundation for automated testing.\n\nWith Storybook 9, we partnered with the latest generation of testing tools to build the ultimate component testing tool. Vitest ships the fastest test runner available. Playwright delivers unmatched browser fidelity. And of course, Storybook is the easiest way to express UI variations. \n\n* ▶️ **Interaction tests**: Verify functionality by simulating user behavior\n* ♿ **Accessibility tests**: Detect, diagnose, and fix WCAG violations\n* 👁️ **Visual tests**: Check for appearance bugs down to the pixel\n* 🛡️ **Coverage reports:** Understand which code is tested at a glance\n* 🚥 **Test widget**: Click to run a comprehensive test suite\n\nAnd core upgrades:\n\n* 🪶 **48% Leaner**: Smaller install with optional docs and test packages\n* ✍️ **Story generation**: Tools to write stories automatically\n* 🏷️ **Tag-based organization:** Filter and group stories by tag\n* 🌐 **Story globals:** Set context (theme, viewport, locale) at the story level\n* 🏗️ **Frameworks**: Major updates for Svelte, Next.js, React Native, and more!\n\n## Say hello to Storybook Test\n\nIn Storybook 9, we teamed up with Vitest, the ecosystem’s fastest test runner, to create a superior tool for testing components. Kick off tests across all your stories at once. Enable \"Watch mode\" to run only the relevant tests when you save a file.\n\n### Why test components?\n\nUnit tests validate logic; E2E tests are best for a few key flows. Storybook Test covers the middle – your components. Component tests hit the sweet spot between the speed of unit tests and the in-browser fidelity of end-to-end (E2E) tests, while avoiding the downsides. \n\nStorybook is the perfect tool for testing components because stories already express every variation, so adding tests to those variations is easy. This allows your test suite to scale to thousands of UI states with minimal maintenance. \n\nTable showing that component tests have good maintenance, iteration speed, and fidelity. Unit tests have good maintenance and iteration speed, but bad fidelity. And end-to-end tests have good fidelity, but bad maintenance and iteration speed.\n\n### The 3 main types of frontend tests\n\nIn frontend development, there are three key dimensions that your users interact with. Storybook runs tests against these dimensions in local development and CI.\n\n1. **Interaction tests** –Does it work?\n2. **Accessibility tests** – Can everyone use it?\n3. **Visual tests** – Does it look right?\n\n### Interaction tests\n\nInteraction tests simulate user behavior and assert that the component functions as expected. Storybook has supported this for years, but you could only run these tests when you navigated to the story. Now you can run all interaction tests across all your stories with a single click and report test statuses in the sidebar. \n\nStorybook showing a passing interaction test with the debugger panel open\n\n### Accessibility tests\n\nAccessibility compliance is essential for modern frontends. But traditional accessibility testing methods are too late, too slow and expensive for too little coverage. Storybook lets you run accessibility tests across all your stories simultaneously and inspect the violations directly in your browser. This way, you catch WCAG violations early in the development cycle. These checks are implemented by &#96;axe-core&#96;, the industry standard tool.\n\nStorybook showing a story with accessibility violations, detailed in both the accessibility addon panel and the highlight menu in the story preview\n\n### Visual tests\n\nVisual bugs ruin even the best frontends. Storybook helps you prevent bugs by scanning all your stories to pinpoint UI changes down to the pixel. Powered by Chromatic, the visual testing cloud service made by Storybook maintainers.\n\nStorybook showing a visual test with a highlighted difference in the visual tests panel\n\n### Test coverage\n\nStorybook’s superpower is that you can test _all_ the UI states in your application, not just happy paths. But how do you know if you've tested everything? That's where test coverage comes in. Compute exactly which lines, functions, and branches are exercised by your component tests.\n\nTwo browser windows. The foreground shows the HTML coverage report. The background shows Storybook after a test run, where you can see the calculated coverage summary.\n\n### Test Widget: Click to test everything \n\nThe Test Widget anchors Storybook Test. Run all tests across all stories—or configure which types to run. You can then filter the sidebar to only show stories with warnings or errors. Each test type has its own debug panel. Since Storybook runs in your own browser, you can also debug using browser dev tools.\n\nStorybook's test widget, showing watch mode activated. Part of the UI says \"Run component tests. Watching for file changes.\"\n\n## Core upgrades \n\n### 48% Leaner\n\nStorybook 9 is less than half the size of Storybook 8 with a flatter dependency structure that prevents conflicts in your &#96;package.json&#96;. The lighter weight also results in a faster install.\n\nA before/after of Storybook's dependency graph. The before is vastly larger and more complex.\n\n### Story generation\n\nStorybook 9’s story generation allows you to create and edit stories from the UI, to capture every state of your component. With the new Test Codegen addon by Igor Luchenkov, you don't need to write code to test your components either. You can record your interactions with your component, add assertions, and save your test... all without leaving Storybook.\n\nAdding a new stories file for a component in Storybook\n\n### Tags-based organization\n\nTags help you to organize and filter stories and components in large Storybooks. Tag stories based on status (&#96;alpha&#96;, &#96;stable&#96;, &#96;deprecated&#96;, etc.), role (&#96;design&#96;, &#96;dev&#96;, &#96;product&#96;), team, feature area, or whatever fits your needs. From there, you can filter the sidebar by tag or even show tags as badges using the Storybook Tag Badges addon by Steve Dodier-Lazaro.\n\nStorybook's sidebar with the filter menu open, showing the available tags to filter on\n\n### Story globals\n\nStory globals let you set context variables—like the **theme**, **viewport**, **locale**, or **background**—on a per-story or per-component basis. That makes it easy to test and document your UI under real conditions: dark mode, mobile view, right-to-left locale, and more.\n\nUsing a story global to toggle different themes\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;typescript\n// Button.stories.ts\nexport default { component: Button };\n\n// Normal story: theme is configurable in UI\nexport const Default = { args: { label: 'Button' } };\n\n// 🌎 Force this story to be in the \"dark\" theme \nexport const Dark = {\n  ...Default,\n  globals: { theme: 'dark' }\n};\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Framework improvements\n\nStorybook supports every major frontend web framework and 9.0 has major quality of life improvements across them all.\n\n### Vite-powered Next.js\n\n@storybook/nextjs-vite is a new, instant-on evolution of Storybook’s Next.js framework. It has the same features (Navigation/Route mocking, Image and Font components, etc.) as its Webpack-based predecessor. But since it’s based on Vite, it provides a modern development experience that is fully compatible with Storybook Test and Vitest.\n\nCLI output when starting Storybook with the &#96;nextjs-vite&#96; framework\n\n### Svelte 5 support\n\nThe Svelte CSF story format has been upgraded to Svelte 5, including support for new language features like runes and snippets.\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;svelte\n\u003cStory name=\"Default\" args={{ exampleProp: true }}\u003e\n  {#snippet template(args)}\n    \u003cMyComponent {...args}\u003eReactive\u003c/MyComponent\u003e\n  {/snippet}\n\u003c/Story\u003e\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n### React Native everywhere\n\nStorybook React Native and React Native Web can now run side-by-side in your mobile project. So you can develop components in full fidelity on devices and simulators. But you can also document and test those same stories using the full feature set of Storybook for Web.\n\nMarcelo Prado's React Native Flash Calendar running side-by-side in both RNW and RN. The RNW Storybook includes the Docs and Test addons. A test run shows that the calendar passes all WCAG accessibility checks!\n\n## Try Storybook 9 today\n\nTry it in a new project:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nnpm create storybook@latest\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nIf you have an existing Storybook project, use our automated migration wizard to help you along the way:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;shell\nnpx storybook@latest upgrade\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nWe also provide a migration guide to help fill in the gaps.\n\n## What’s next?\n\nWith overwhelmingly positive pre-release responses to Storybook Test and our bundle size reductions, we plan to double down in 9.x.\n\n* ESM-only to further reduce install size and complexity\n* Streamlined module mocking\n* Better typesafety and autocompletion for stories\n\nFor an up-to-date view on what we’re working on, check out Storybook’s roadmap.\n\n## Credits\n\n### Core team\n\nMichael Arestad, Yann Braga, João Cardoso, Tom Coleman, Norbert de Langen, Kyle Gach, Gert Hengeveld, Dom Nguyen, Valentin Palkovic, Kasper Peulen, Jeppe Reinhold, Lars Rickert, Kai Röder, Michael Shilman (me!), Varun Vachhar, Ian Van Schooten, Daniel Williams, Josh Wooding, and Vanessa Yuen\n\n### Contributors\n\n@acusti @agentender @alirezaebrahimkhani @ashphy @audie80 @b0g3r @benmccann @dannyhw @dummdidumm @edbzn @fi3ework @filipemelo2002 @flaval @gchqdeveloper548 @ghengeveld @guria @hakshu25 @iineineno03k @irinaklimova @jamesives @jonniebigodes @jreinhold @jsmike @kasperpeulen @kenrick95 @kroeder @kylegach @larsrickert @laupetin @leeovictor @leoeuclids @makotot @masstronaut @mrginglymus @muhdhishamp @ndelangen @netroy @notwoods @okathira @rchaoz @robertisaac @sentience @shilman @sidnioulz @sookmax @spanishpear @tmeasday @tomkalina @valentinpalkovic @vanessayuenn @webpro @wlewis-formative @xeho91 @yannbf @yatishgoel\n\n\u003e Storybook 9 is here! Controls\n\nReactVueAngularWeb ComponentsMore\n\nStorybook Controls gives you a graphical UI to interact with a component's arguments dynamically without needing to code. Use the Controls panel to edit the inputs to your stories and see the results in real-time. It's a great way to explore your components and test different states.\n\nControls do not require any modification to your components. Stories for controls are:\n\n* Convenient. Auto-generate controls based on React/Vue/Angular/etc. components.\n* Portable. Reuse your interactive stories in documentation, tests, and even in designs.\n* Rich. Customize the controls and interactive data to suit your exact needs.\n\nTo use Controls, you need to write your stories using args. Storybook will automatically generate UI controls based on your args and what it can infer about your component. Still, you can configure the controls further using argTypes, see below.\n\n💡\n\nIf you have stories in the older pre-Storybook 6 style, check the args \u0026 controls migration guide to learn how to convert your existing stories for args.\n\n## Choosing the control type\n\nBy default, Storybook will choose a control for each arg based on its initial value. This will work well with specific arg types (e.g., &#96;boolean&#96; or &#96;string&#96;). To enable them, add the &#96;component&#96; annotation to the default export of your story file, and it will be used to infer the controls and auto-generate the matching argTypes for your component using react-docgen, a documentation generator for React components that also includes first-class support for TypeScript.\n\nButton.stories.ts|tsx\n\nTypescript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// Replace your-framework with the framework you are using, e.g. react-vite, nextjs, nextjs-vite, etc.\nimport type { Meta } from '@storybook/your-framework';\n \nimport { Button } from './Button';\n \nconst meta = {\n  component: Button,\n} satisfies Meta\u003ctypeof Button\u003e;\n \nexport default meta;\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nFor instance, suppose you have a &#96;variant&#96; arg on your story that should be &#96;primary&#96; or &#96;secondary&#96;:\n\nButton.stories.ts|tsx\n\nTypescript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// Replace your-framework with the framework you are using, e.g. react-vite, nextjs, vue3-vite, etc.\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/your-framework';\n \nimport { Button } from './Button';\n \nconst meta = {\n  component: Button,\n} satisfies Meta\u003ctypeof Button\u003e;\n \nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof meta\u003e;\n \nexport const Primary: Story = {\n  args: {\n    variant: 'primary',\n  },\n};\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nBy default, Storybook will render a free text input for the &#96;variant&#96; arg:\n\nControl using a string\n\nIt works as long as you type a valid string into the auto-generated text control. Still, it's not the best UI for our scenario, given that the component only accepts &#96;primary&#96; or &#96;secondary&#96; as variants. Let’s replace it with Storybook’s radio component.\n\nWe can specify which controls get used by declaring a custom argType for the &#96;variant&#96; property. ArgTypes encode basic metadata for args, such as name, description, and defaultValue for an arg. These get automatically filled in by Storybook Docs.\n\n&#96;ArgTypes&#96; can also contain arbitrary annotations, which the user can override. Since &#96;variant&#96; is a component property, let's put that annotation on the default export.\n\nButton.stories.ts|tsx\n\nTypescript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// Replace your-framework with the framework you are using, e.g. react-vite, nextjs, vue3-vite, etc.\nimport type { Meta } from '@storybook/your-framework';\n \nimport { Button } from './Button';\n \nconst meta = {\n  component: Button,\n  argTypes: {\n    variant: {\n      options: ['primary', 'secondary'],\n      control: { type: 'radio' },\n    },\n  },\n} satisfies Meta\u003ctypeof Button\u003e;\n \nexport default meta;\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n💡\n\nArgTypes are a powerful feature that can be used to customize the controls for your stories. For more information, see the documentation about customizing controls with &#96;argTypes&#96; annotation.\n\nThis replaces the input with a radio group for a more intuitive experience.\n\nControl with a radio group\n\n## Custom control type matchers\n\nControls can automatically be inferred from arg's name with regex, but currently only for the color picker and date picker controls. If you've used the Storybook CLI to setup your project, it should have automatically created the following defaults in &#96;.storybook/preview.js|ts&#96;:\n\n| Control   | Default regex           | Description                                               |\n| --------- | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |\n| **color** | /(background\\|color)$/i | Will display a color picker UI for the args that match it |\n| **date**  | /Date$/                 | Will display a date picker UI for the args that match it  |\n\nIf you haven't used the CLI to set the configuration, or if you want to define your patterns, use the &#96;matchers&#96; property in the &#96;controls&#96; parameter:\n\n.storybook/preview.ts\n\nTypescript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// Replace your-framework with the framework you are using, e.g. react-vite, nextjs, vue3-vite, etc.\nimport type { Preview } from '@storybook/your-framework';\n \nconst preview: Preview = {\n  parameters: {\n    controls: {\n      matchers: {\n        color: /(background|color)$/i,\n        date: /Date$/,\n      },\n    },\n  },\n};\n \nexport default preview;\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Fully custom args\n\nUntil now, we only used auto-generated controls based on the component for which we're writing stories. If we are writing complex stories, we may want to add controls for args that aren’t part of the component. For example, here's how you could use a &#96;footer&#96; arg to populate a child component:\n\nPage.stories.ts|tsx\n\nTypescript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// Replace your-framework with the framework you are using, e.g. react-vite, nextjs, nextjs-vite, etc.\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/your-framework';\n \nimport { Page } from './Page';\n \ntype PagePropsAndCustomArgs = React.ComponentProps\u003ctypeof Page\u003e \u0026 { footer?: string };\n \nconst meta = {\n  component: Page,\n  render: ({ footer, ...args }) =\u003e (\n    \u003cPage {...args}\u003e\n      \u003cfooter\u003e{footer}\u003c/footer\u003e\n    \u003c/Page\u003e\n  ),\n} satisfies Meta\u003cPagePropsAndCustomArgs\u003e;\nexport default meta;\n \ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof meta\u003e;\n \nexport const CustomFooter = {\n  args: {\n    footer: 'Built with Storybook',\n  },\n} satisfies Story;\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nBy default, Storybook will add controls for all args that:\n\n* It infers from the component definition if your framework supports it.\n* Appear in the list of args for your story.\n\nUsing &#96;argTypes&#96;, you can change the display and behavior of each control.\n\n### Dealing with complex values\n\nWhen dealing with non-primitive values, you'll notice that you'll run into some limitations. The most obvious issue is that not every value can be represented as part of the &#96;args&#96; param in the URL, losing the ability to share and deep link to such a state. Beyond that, complex values such as JSX cannot be synchronized between the manager (e.g., the Controls panel) and the preview (your story).\n\nOne way to deal with this is to use primitive values (e.g., strings) as arg values and add a custom &#96;render&#96; function to convert them to their complex counterpart before rendering. It isn't the nicest way to do it (see below), but certainly the most flexible.\n\nYourComponent.stories.ts|tsx\n\nTypescript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// Replace your-framework with the framework you are using, e.g. react-vite, nextjs, nextjs-vite, etc.\nimport type { Meta, StoryObj } from '@storybook/your-framework';\n \nimport { YourComponent } from './your-component';\n \nconst meta = {\n  component: YourComponent,\n  //👇 Creates specific argTypes with options\n  argTypes: {\n    propertyA: {\n      options: ['Item One', 'Item Two', 'Item Three'],\n      control: { type: 'select' }, // Automatically inferred when 'options' is defined\n    },\n    propertyB: {\n      options: ['Another Item One', 'Another Item Two', 'Another Item Three'],\n    },\n  },\n} satisfies Meta\u003ctypeof YourComponent\u003e;\n \nexport default meta;\ntype Story = StoryObj\u003ctypeof meta\u003e;\n \nconst someFunction = (valuePropertyA, valuePropertyB) =\u003e {\n  // Do some logic here\n};\n \nexport const ExampleStory: Story = {\n  render: (args) =\u003e {\n    const { propertyA, propertyB } = args;\n    //👇 Assigns the function result to a variable\n    const someFunctionResult = someFunction(propertyA, propertyB);\n \n    return \u003cYourComponent {...args} someProperty={someFunctionResult} /\u003e;\n  },\n  args: {\n    propertyA: 'Item One',\n    propertyB: 'Another Item One',\n  },\n};\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nUnless you need the flexibility of a function, an easier way to map primitives to complex values before rendering is to define a &#96;mapping&#96;; additionally, you can specify &#96;control.labels&#96; to configure custom labels for your checkbox, radio, or select input.\n\nButton.stories.ts|tsx\n\nTypescript\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n// Replace your-framework with the framework you are using, e.g. react-vite, nextjs, vue3-vite, etc.\nimport type { Meta } from '@storybook/your-framework';\n \nimport { Button } from './Button';\n \nimport { ArrowUp, ArrowDown, ArrowLeft, ArrowRight } from './icons';\n \nconst arrows = { ArrowUp, ArrowDown, ArrowLeft, ArrowRight };\n \nconst meta = {\n  component: Button,\n  argTypes: {\n    arrow: {\n      options: Object.keys(arrows), // An array of serializable values\n      mapping: arrows, // Maps serializable option values to complex arg values\n      control: {\n        type: 'select', // Type 'select' is automatically inferred when 'options' is defined\n        labels: {\n          // 'labels' maps option values to string labels\n          ArrowUp: 'Up',\n          ArrowDown: 'Down',\n          ArrowLeft: 'Left',\n          ArrowRight: 'Right',\n        },\n      },\n    },\n  },\n} satisfies Meta\u003ctypeof Button\u003e;\n \nexport default meta;\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nNote that both &#96;mapping&#96; and &#96;control.labels&#96; don't have to be exhaustive. If the currently selected option is not listed, it's used verbatim.\n\n## Creating and editing stories from controls\n\nYou can create or edit stories, directly from the Controls panel.\n\n### Create a new story\n\nOpen the Controls panel for a story and adjust the value of a control. Then save those changes as a new story.\n\nIf you're working on a component that does not yet have any stories, you can click the ➕ button in the sidebar to search for your component and have a basic story created for you.\n\n### Edit a story\n\nYou can also update a control's value, then save the changes to the story. The story file's code will be updated for you.\n\n### Disable creating and editing of stories\n\nIf you don't want to allow the creation or editing of stories from the Controls panel, you can disable this feature by setting the &#96;disableSaveFromUI&#96; parameter to &#96;true&#96; in the &#96;parameters.controls&#96; parameter in your &#96;.storybook/preview.js|ts&#96; file.\n\n## Configuration\n\nControls can be configured in two ways:\n\n* Individual controls can be configured via control annotations.\n* The panel's appearance can be configured via parameters.\n\n### Annotation\n\nAs shown above, you can configure individual controls with the “control\" annotation in the argTypes field of either a component or story. Below is a condensed example and table featuring all available controls.\n\n| Data Type    | Control                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Description                                                                                                                                       |\n| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| **boolean**  | boolean                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Provides a toggle for switching between possible states. argTypes: { active: { control: 'boolean' }}                                              |\n| **number**   | number                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Provides a numeric input to include the range of all possible values. argTypes: { even: { control: { type: 'number', min:1, max:30, step: 2 } }}  |\n| range        | Provides a range slider component to include all possible values. argTypes: { odd: { control: { type: 'range', min: 1, max: 30, step: 3 } }}                                                                    |                                                                                                         | Provides a JSON-based editor component to handle the object's values. Also allows edition in raw mode. argTypes: { user: { control: 'object' }}   |\n| **array**    | object                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Provides a JSON-based editor component to handle the array's values.
